articles.title: Veja a entrevista de Sanderson (PL) à RBS TV | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do PL ao Senado participa da segunda entrevista ao vivo da série do Bom Dia Rio Grande nesta terça-feira (15).
articles.summary: Em entrevista à RBS TV, o candidato Sanderson (PL) detalhou propostas sobre combate ao feminicídio, dívida do RS e mudanças no STF para as eleições ao Senado.
articles.body:
O candidato do PL ao Senado pelo Rio Grande do Sul, Ubiratan Sanderson, afirmou nesta terça-feira (15), em entrevista ao Bom Dia Rio Grande, que defende o uso de segurança pessoal para mulheres ameaçadas em casos considerados de maior risco .

Segundo Sanderson, o poder público deveria classificar o nível de ameaça enfrentado pelas vítimas e disponibilizar a proteção de policiais em determinadas situações. O candidato também propôs recursos para que mulheres vulneráveis possam deixar suas casas e permanecer em locais seguros.

"Então, o Estado precisa fazer essa classificação primeiro, níveis de ameaça. E, se for o caso, eu acho que é o caso, fazer segurança pessoal para situações que tais, situações mais concretas", afirmou.

Sanderson também falou sobre a dívida do Rio Grande do Sul com a União, prevenção a enchentes , mudanças no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) e revisão da escala de trabalho 6x1 . A entrevista teve duração de 15 minutos.

Ubiratan Antunes Sanderson tem 56 anos. É natural de Erechim, mas se criou em Santo Ângelo. Advogado, fez carreira na Polícia Federal, onde atuou por 23 anos. Estreou na política em 2018, quando foi eleito deputado federal. Nas eleições de 2022, foi reeleito para o cargo.

A entrevista integra a série do Bom Dia Rio Grande com os candidatos ao Senado nas eleições de 2026 . Os candidatos de partidos, coligações e federações que possuem pelo menos cinco representantes no Congresso Nacional participam ao vivo. Os demais são entrevistados em reportagens gravadas.

A ordem foi definida em sorteio na presença dos representantes dos candidatos. As entrevistas ao vivo têm duração de 15 minutos. Veja o calendário:

15 de setembro: Sanderson (PL), ao vivo;

16 de setembro: Milton Cardoso (PSDB), ao vivo;

17 de setembro: entrevistas gravadas com Ric Jones (PCO), Regis Ethur (PSTU), Luciano do MLB (UP) e Daniela Maidana da Silva (PSTU);

18 de setembro: Manuela D'Avila (PSOL), ao vivo;

21 de setembro: Paulo Pimenta (PT), ao vivo;

22 de setembro: Renato Jaguarão (Cidadania), ao vivo;

23 de setembro: Germano Rigotto (MDB), ao vivo;

24 de setembro: Marcel Van Hattem (NOVO), ao vivo.

Sanderson defendeu que o poder público classifique o nível de risco enfrentado por mulheres ameaçadas e disponibilize segurança pessoal nos casos considerados mais graves. O candidato afirmou que a atuação legislativa não é suficiente para impedir os crimes.

Segundo Sanderson, as prefeituras, os governos estaduais e o governo federal precisam investir na rede de proteção. Ele também defendeu recursos para que mulheres sem condições financeiras possam sair de casa e permanecer em hotéis ou outros locais seguros.

"A rede de proteção nessa questão do enfrentamento e no combate e na prevenção ao feminicídio é falha. Não há um investimento concreto com recursos públicos e isso precisa ser feito", afirmou.

Questionado se a proposta retiraria policiais das ruas, Sanderson disse que já existem agentes destinados à proteção de políticos. Para ele, a mesma prioridade deve ser aplicada às mulheres que tenham registrado sucessivas ameaças.

"A ameaçada vai na delegacia de polícia, faz o registro e ganha um papel. Aquele papel é a proteção dela. Um papel não protege ninguém", disse.

Sanderson afirmou que pretende atuar pela prorrogação da suspensão do pagamento das parcelas da dívida do Rio Grande do Sul com a União. Segundo ele, a situação fiscal limita investimentos estaduais em infraestrutura, saúde, educação e segurança pública.

O candidato defendeu uma atuação conjunta dos senadores e deputados federais gaúchos para renegociar a dívida. Ele também propôs a realização de uma auditoria para verificar a origem, o tamanho e os juros aplicados ao débito.

"Nós vamos ter que prorrogar. Isso passa pelo Congresso, passa pelo Senado, passa pela Câmara", afirmou.

Sanderson sugeriu que a auditoria seja conduzida pelo Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU) ou pelo Tesouro Nacional. Segundo ele, o procedimento também deveria ter a participação dos representantes do Rio Grande do Sul no Congresso Nacional, do governador e da população.

"Eu sou adepto, inclusive, a uma auditoria, verificar qual é o tamanho da dívida, talvez uma revisional de juros, e, com isso, darmos possibilidade do nosso Estado parar com essa evasão de investidores, evasão de cidadãos do Rio Grande do Sul, que têm ido para outros estados", disse.

Questionado sobre a obtenção de recursos para obras de prevenção a enchentes, Sanderson afirmou que pretende propor mudanças na legislação ambiental. Segundo o candidato, as regras atuais dificultam a execução de medidas pelos governos estadual e municipais.

Sanderson afirmou que os prefeitos deveriam participar de forma mais ativa das ações de prevenção. Ele citou visitas a municípios do Vale do Taquari e disse que destinou emendas parlamentares a cidades atingidas pelas enchentes.

O candidato criticou a discussão entre o presidente da República e o governador do Rio Grande do Sul sobre a responsabilidade pela execução das obras. Segundo Sanderson, recursos foram encaminhados, mas medidas de prevenção ainda não foram concluídas.

"Nós precisamos mudar a legislação ambiental, que ela é proibitiva de qualquer tipo de salvaguarda para a população aqui do Rio Grande do Sul", disse.

Sanderson defendeu o estabelecimento de mandatos para ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal e a indicação exclusiva de magistrados de carreira para o tribunal. O candidato citou uma proposta do senador Carlos Portinho, do PL do Rio de Janeiro.

Segundo Sanderson, as mudanças fariam parte de uma reforma mais ampla do sistema de Justiça. O candidato afirmou que a indicação apenas de juízes concursados reduziria a influência do presidente da República na escolha dos ministros.

"Nós temos uma proposta do senador Carlos Portinho, do PL do Rio de Janeiro, que estabelece a reforma do sistema de Justiça brasileira, como um todo. E aí estabelece mandato para os ministros do STF, indicação apenas de magistrados de carreira, de juízes concursados", afirmou.

Sanderson também disse que pretende apresentar pedidos de abertura de processos de impeachment contra pelo menos três ministros do STF caso seja eleito. O único integrante do tribunal mencionado nominalmente pelo candidato foi Alexandre de Moraes.

"No Senado, no primeiro dia, eu estando no Senado, quero apresentar pedidos de abertura de processo de impeachment em pelo menos três ministros do STF, inclusive desse ministro Alexandre Moraes", disse.

Sanderson lembrou que votou a favor de uma proposta relacionada ao fim da escala de trabalho 6x1 na Câmara dos Deputados. Segundo o candidato, no entanto, a medida precisa ser aprimorada para considerar os interesses de trabalhadores e empregadores.

"Nós precisamos aprimorar essa medida e, por isso, também temos uma proposta já em andamento no Senado Federal, proposta apresentada pelo senador Rogério Marinho, que busca fazer a flexibilização do regime de trabalho", afirmou.

Sanderson classificou a proposta conduzida pelo governo federal como eleitoreira e populista. Segundo ele, o caminho deve ser a modernização das relações de trabalho.

"Agora, no Senado, nós temos condições de atuar pela modernização efetiva e a modernização diz respeito à flexibilização do regime de trabalho e nisso que nós vamos apostar", disse.

Sanderson, candidato ao Senado do PL pelo Rio Grande do Sul — Foto: Reprodução/RBS TV

articles.title: Dino pede a Fachin investigação sobre elo entre Banco Master e instituto ligado a André Mendonça | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministro quer esclarecer possíveis conexões entre encontro de Vorcaro com Mendonça, contratos do Instituto Iter e processo sobre cemitérios privados.
articles.summary: Ministro quer esclarecer possíveis conexões entre encontro de Vorcaro com Mendonça, contratos do Instituto Iter e processo sobre cemitérios privados.
articles.body:
O ministro Flávio Dino, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), pediu nesta terça-feira (15) ao presidente da Corte, Edson Fachin, que seja investigada uma possível relação entre o Banco Master, o Instituto Iter — ligado ao ministro André Mendonça —, e contratos firmados pelo município de São Paulo.

A decisão de Dino é relacionada a uma ação que discute regras para o funcionamento de cemitérios privados no estado . O ministro cita uma série de circunstâncias que, na avaliação dele, precisam ser esclarecidas.

O primeiro ponto envolve a atuação de André Mendonça em um processo sobre os cemitérios privados de São Paulo.

Quando o julgamento foi retomado, em abril de 2025, Mendonça apresentou um voto contrário à manutenção de uma medida cautelar que afetava os cemitérios privados. Com isso, ficou alinhado aos pedidos dessas empresas.

Ao analisar o caso, Dino chamou atenção para o fato de que Alexandre de Almeida Mendonça, irmão de André Mendonça, trabalha na SP Regula, agência responsável pela regulação de serviços públicos de São Paulo. O irmão atua justamente na área funerária e cemiterial.

Dino também cita um encontro entre André Mendonça e Daniel Vorcaro, dono do extinto Banco Master.

Segundo a decisão, a reunião ocorreu em 14 de março de 2025, na sede do Instituto Iter, entidade fundada por Mendonça.

Para Dino, o encontro ganha relevância porque o Instituto Iter passou a ter contratos remunerados com o município de São Paulo, que é parte diretamente envolvida na ação sobre os cemitérios.

Segundo a decisão, o Instituto Iter passou a prestar serviços para o município de São Paulo . A prefeitura, por sua vez, é responsável pela contratação de empresas privadas que atuam no setor funerário, como a Cortel.

Na decisão, Dino cita ainda Fabiano Zettel — cunhado de Vorcaro e também investigado na Operação Compliance Zero —, que trabalhava na Cortel.

Além desse contrato, o ministro afirma que o Instituto Iter também teria firmado, sem licitação, um contrato de aproximadamente R$ 1,63 milhão com a Fundação para o Desenvolvimento da Educação (FDE), ligada ao governo de São Paulo.

O contrato seria para a prestação de serviços técnicos na área de formação e gestão educacional.

A partir desses fatos, o ministro diz que o objetivo da decisão é esclarecer se existe alguma relação entre o encontro de Vorcaro com Mendonça, o Instituto Iter, os contratos mantidos pela entidade e a atuação de Mendonça no processo que envolve os cemitérios privados de São Paulo.

A decisão não afirma que esses fatos, por si só, comprovem irregularidade ou favorecimento por parte de Mendonça.

O pedido de Dino é para que as possíveis conexões sejam apuradas.

articles.title: Polícia faz segunda fase de operação que investiga morte de menina transmitida em rede social | G1
articles.standfirst: Mandados são contra seis adolescentes suspeitos de envolvimento na morte de de adolescente de 13 anos.
articles.summary: Mandados são contra seis adolescentes suspeitos de envolvimento na morte de de adolescente de 13 anos.
articles.body:
Policiais civis cumprem nesta terça-feira (15) mandados contra seis adolescentes suspeitos de envolvimento na morte de uma menina de 13 anos que foi transmitida durante uma “live” no Discord.

Os mandados de internação e de busca e apreensão estão sendo cumpridos nos estados do Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Bahia, Rio Grande do Sul e no Distrito Federal. Os alvos têm entre 14 e 17 anos, segundo informações obtidas pela TV Globo .

🔎O Discord é uma plataforma de comunicação bastante utilizada por jogadores de games online e também por adolescentes. A empresa tem sido alvo de críticas e investigações relacionadas a falhas na moderação de conteúdo e na verificação da idade dos usuários.

Essa é a segunda fase da chamada Operação Lívia , que recebe o nome da vítima que, segundo a polícia, tirou a própria vida, em julho, depois de ser induzida por participantes de um grupo na rede social.

Na primeira fase, que aconteceu no início de agosto, um adulto foi preso e outros cinco adolescentes apreendidos, entre eles um adolescente de 14 anos considerado o líder do grupo. Ao todo, 11 pessoas foram presas e apreendidas responsabilizadas pelo caso.

A investigação é da Polícia Civil do Mato Grosso do Sul e conta com o apoio do Laboratório de Operações Cibernéticas (Ciberlab), ligado ao Ministério da Justiça.

De acordo com a investigação, os alvos dessa segunda fase são suspeitos de integrar uma rede que usa plataformas digitais para a prática de crueldade contra animais e para coagir crianças e adolescentes.

Segundo os investigadores, a análise do material apreendido na primeira fase — computadores, celulares e outras mídias — possibilitou o avanço investigativo e a identificação de novos envolvidos, administradores e moderadores das comunidades investigadas.

As transmissões ao vivo do Discord foram suspensas no Brasil após a Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) identificar que a ferramenta vinha sendo usada de forma recorrente em casos de violência, assédio e indução à automutilação e ao suicídio envolvendo crianças e adolescentes.

No início deste mês de setembro, a plataforma e o governo participaram de uma audiência de conciliação, realizada pela Justiça Federal do Distrito Federal.

A audiência foi marcada após a Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU) apresentar uma ação para que a plataforma Discord adote medidas efetivas para proteger crianças, adolescentes e mulheres no ambiente digital, de acordo com as exigências da legislação brasileira, em especial as estabelecidas pelo ECA Digital.

A ação pede ainda que o Discord seja condenado a pagar uma indenização por danos morais no valor de R$ 500 milhões.

O governo entrou com a ação após identificar que a plataforma continua apresentando falhas nos mecanismos proteção aos usuários.

articles.title: Dr. Zacharias Calil defende VLT no Entorno e fim da escala 6x1 | G1
articles.standfirst: O candidato destacou sua atuação na Saúde, falou sobre sua opinião sobre a PEC pelo fim da Escala 6x1 e emendas PIX. O Bom Dia Goiás entrevista 5 candidatos ao Senado nesta semana.
articles.summary: O candidato destacou sua atuação na Saúde, falou sobre sua opinião sobre a PEC pelo fim da Escala 6x1 e emendas PIX. O Bom Dia Goiás entrevista 5 candidatos ao Senado nesta semana.
articles.body:
Zacharias Calil (MDB), candidato ao Senado, é entrevistado no Bom Dia Goiás — Foto: Reprodução/TV Anhanguera

Na manhã desta terça-feira (15), a TV Anhanguera recebeu o Dr. Zacharias Calil (MDB), candidato ao Senado por Goiás. Zacharias falou sobre sua mudança de partido, atuação na área da Saúde, sua opinião sobre a PEC pelo fim da escala 6x1, emendas PIX e ainda a proposta da criação de um Veículo Leve sobre Trilhos (VLT) no Entorno do Distrito Federal (DF). O g1 Goiás transmitiu a entrevista ao vivo.

Esta foi a primeira de uma série de entrevistas do Bom Dia Goiás com os candidatos ao Senado. Foram convidados os candidatos com 5% ou mais das intenções de voto na última pesquisa Quaest. As entrevistas têm como objetivo aprofundar as propostas dos candidatos e discutir temas de interesse da população. As entrevistas têm duração de 15 minutos.

Confira os temas discutidos na entrevista:

Mudança de partido e resultado da última pesquisa

Na última pesquisa Quaest, o médico apareceu com 9% das intenções de voto, empatado tecnicamente com Vanderlan Cardoso, da base aliada, atrás de Gracinha Caiado e Gustavo Gayer. Sobre isso, Zacharias disse que houve um "problema político" com a base aliada quando mudou de partido e que, em sua opinião, o novo partido não errou em lançar quatro candidatos, pois o processo é democrático.

Zacharias construiu sua trajetória política em torno da Saúde. Na entrevista, ele disse que é titular da Comissão de Saúde da Câmara Federal e que trabalhou no melhoramento da tabela SUSque, segundo ele, está defasada. Disse ainda que é preciso trazer os especialistas para mais perto da população e que "zerar a fila" é quase impossível, mas prioridades precisam ser definidas.

Sobre o fato de ter um mandato muito focado na Saúde, o Dr. Zacharias Calil disse que 50% das emendas parlamentares precisam ser destinadas à Saúde e que existem outras bancadas com projetos específicos, como no caso da evangélica e do agronegócio. Em contrapartida, ele diz que, no Senado, trabalhará para levar os projetos de lei na infraestrutura, no orçamento e em mais setores da articulação federativa.

O Dr. Zacharias Calil assinou a PEC pelo fim da escala 6X1 e chegou a apoiar uma emenda de transição mais longa, mas voltou atrás. Durante a conversa, ele disse que é a favor da jornada de 44 horas e que, nesse processo, houve uma discussão com empresários, mas que ele começou a se preocupar com a saúde do trabalhador.

Sobre a federalização da Segurança Pública, Zacharias disse que os estados e governadores devem ter autonomia na pasta. Em 2018, o candidato havia defendido o modelo de federalização, mas explicou por que voltou atrás. Disse ainda que deve melhorar a estrutura das polícias com a destinação de emendas, por exemplo.

Sobre as chamadas "emendas PIX", emendas individuais de transferência especial, Dr. Zacharias Calil disse que destinou apenas uma emenda com essa modalidade. Disse ainda que uma nova decisão do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) aumentou a transparência nas emendas.

Em relação ao transporte público na região do Entorno do Distrito Federal (DF), o Dr. Zacharias Calil disse que pretende propor verba para a construção de um Veículo Leve sobre Trilhos (VLT) que possa ligar Brasília (DF) às cidades do Entorno.

O candidato pediu que a população vote "consciente". Disse ainda que trabalha há 40 anos no serviço público, colocando o Estado de Goiás e o Brasil a nível internacional.

articles.title: Daniel Vorcaro: defesa aguarda decisão do STF para nova estratégia | G1
articles.standfirst: Defesa do ex-banqueiro aguarda o resultado da sessão desta terça-feira para decidir os próximos passos; expectativa é que decisão influencie eventual nova tentativa de acordo de colaboração.
articles.summary: Daniel Vorcaro aguarda sessão do STF nesta terça-feira para definir novos passos da defesa e uma possível tentativa de acordo de delação premiada.
articles.body:
A sessão desta terça-feira (15) no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) é vista por pessoas próximas ao banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro como um marco para os rumos de sua estratégia de defesa. A avaliação é que o julgamento poderá trazer uma definição importante sobre a condução de processos relacionados ao caso e, consequentemente, influenciar os próximos movimentos jurídicos do empresário.

Nos bastidores, interlocutores de Vorcaro afirmam que a orientação da defesa, neste momento, é aguardar o desfecho da sessão antes de tomar qualquer decisão. A cautela se explica pela indefinição sobre quem ficará responsável, em caráter permanente ou temporário, por questões relacionadas ao caso envolvendo o Banco Master.

Daniel Vorcaro ficará preso em cela de 6 m² de presídio de segurança máxima em Brasília — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

A expectativa também está ligada às tentativas de negociação de um acordo de colaboração premiada. Segundo relatos de pessoas que acompanham as discussões, propostas anteriores teriam sido rejeitadas pela Polícia Federal. Com a troca de advogados e a reorganização da equipe jurídica, uma nova investida não está descartada.

Outro fator que pesa na análise da defesa é a situação dos ativos nos quais Vorcaro investiu nos últimos anos. O banqueiro já reconheceu publicamente que apostou nesses investimentos como estratégia de proteção patrimonial e aguardava retorno financeiro dessas operações.

Até recentemente, defesa do empresário trabalhava com a perspectiva de um cenário de acomodação política e institucional após as eleições. A percepção, porém, começou a mudar diante dos desdobramentos mais recentes e da possibilidade de alterações no ambiente jurídico em Brasília.

Preso, Vorcaro acompanha atentamente os acontecimentos por meio de sua equipe e de pessoas de confiança. A avaliação é que eventuais propostas de colaboração apresentadas até agora teriam preservado nomes considerados centrais ou de maior relevância política e institucional.

A expectativa é que o resultado funcione como um termômetro para os próximos passos de Vorcaro e de seus advogados.

articles.title: Surrogate who refused abortion asks SCOTUS to intervene as baby could be moved out of Texas
articles.summary: Surrogate McKenna West asked the Supreme Court for an emergency administrative stay, fearing the newborn could be moved from Texas to California.
articles.body: The surrogate who refused an abortion sought by the biological parents has filed an updated brief with the U.S. Supreme Court following an emergency application she filed with the court last week, arguing the case is moving more quickly than expected. McKenna West, an Alaska resident, and a California couple referred to as the commissioning parties, have been involved in a legal battle after she refused their request to terminate the pregnancy after a diagnosis of a serious heart condition, hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS). Represented by attorneys from Alliance Defending Freedom and First & Fourteenth PLLC, West asked Justice Elena Kagan, who handles emergency matters from the Ninth Circuit, for an administrative stay and a stay pending a possible petition for certiorari. SURROGATE, CALIFORNIA COUPLE CLASH IN COURT AS NEWBORN FIGHTS FOR LIFE AFTER HEART SURGERY Her application argues that the California courts violated federal due process by treating her jurisdictional defense as consent. It also argues that without a stay, the baby could be moved to California for hospice care while West remains unable to participate in decisions about the child's medical treatment. But on Monday, the surrogate and her team expressed fears that the baby may be moved out of Texas earlier than she had expected. She is asking the high court for an administrative stay 1 p.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday. SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION This comes after a California court judgment that declared the commissioning parents the child's legal parents and denied West's custody claims. The commissioning parents have argued in court that California has jurisdiction under the surrogacy agreement and that they are the child's legal parents. West had refused the commissioning parents' request for an abortion and traveled to Texas, which has abortion restrictions, to give birth, saying she did so to ensure access to specialized medical care. She asked for parentage and protective orders in Alaska and Texas, but the commissioning parents filed a parentage action in the Los Angeles Superior Court, according to Fox 4. West entered a special appearance to contest personal jurisdiction and object to the forum, citing a forum-selection clause that required litigation to be held in Alaska. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But the California trial court ruled that West’s jurisdictional arguments and attached exhibits constituted a general appearance, meaning she had consented to the court’s jurisdiction, the outlet reported. The court then entered an ex parte judgment of parentage in favor of the commissioning parents. After the baby was born in Texas on Aug. 12, a Texas court recognized the California ruling naming the commissioning couple as his legal parents and dismissed West from the case with prejudice, meaning she could not refile the same claim in that proceeding.

articles.title: Mitch McConnell returns to US Senate after three-month absence
articles.summary: Senator McConnell casts his first vote since June, pledging presence for crucial Senate decisions.
articles.body:
United States Senator Mitch McConnell has returned to Congress, casting his vote for the first time since he was hospitalised three months ago after a fall in his home in Washington, raising questions about his ability to serve.

“I must admit. After two years of – decades, actually – dodging your questions, I wasn’t sure how many of you would be here today. But I’m glad to see you. Time to get back to work, finish the job for this Congress,” McConnell told reporters outside the Senate chamber on Monday.

The disappearance from public view of the 84-year-old Kentucky Republican raised many questions within the Republican Party.

But he put the speculation to rest on Monday in a statement on social media announcing his return.

“Today, I’ll cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June,” he wrote on X. “I’m really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues.”

He said he is “not quite back to 100%”, adding that the lingering effects of “childhood polio” made his recovery difficult, but he assured his colleagues that he will do his “best to be present” for tough votes “when our conference needs me”.

There were growing worries within the Republican Party that his absence would negatively affect it, as the party holds a narrow 53-47 majority in the Senate.

Democrats have already used his absence to pass a resolution against US President Donald Trump’s war with Iran, as four Republicans also broke from the party to support the resolution.

McConnell is the longest-serving Senate leader in US history. He announced early last year that he will not be standing for an eighth term.

Kentucky’s Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, raised questions about McConnell’s ability to continue serving his final term that ends January 2027.

images.caption: Senator Mitch McConnell returns home following a vote on the Senate floor after being out of the public eye for more than three months in Washington, DC [Daniel Heuer/Reuters]

articles.title: Raucous primary season reaches final act in deep-blue stronghold, kickstarting sprint to November
articles.summary: Delaware's final 2026 primary caps a season when Donald Trump's endorsements dominated GOP races and progressive socialists ousted incumbents.
articles.body: Delaware voters head to the polls Tuesday for the final primary of the 2026 election cycle, capping a season marked by high-profile victories for progressives and socialists over Democratic establishment rivals and President Donald Trump’s continued immense influence in Republican contests, despite some notable setbacks. Democratic Sen. Chris Coons and state Attorney General Kathy Jennings each face primary opponents, and Democratic Rep. Sarah McBride is unopposed in her primary, as they tune up for the general election, when Republicans will try to break the Democrats' lock on Delaware's statewide offices. Delaware's nominating contests close out a primary season that upended the Democratic Party, with left-wing and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-backed contenders winning and, in some cases, ousting longtime incumbents. A year after socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani rocked the political world with a Democratic primary victory en route to winning the general election in the nation's most populist city, the far-left struck again in June. CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS A slew of incumbents and establishment candidates were defeated by left-wing rivals, including DSA members Melat Kiros topping 15-term incumbent Democratic Rep. Diana DeGette of Colorado and Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York ousting five-term Democratic Rep. Adriano Espaillat of New York. Those wins were followed on an even larger scale in August, with triumphs in crucial statewide Senate primaries by Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota and state Rep. Angie Nixon in Florida. While there were notable setbacks for the left, including frontrunner Francesca Hong's August defeat in battleground Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial primary, the left vastly increased its clout in the political fight for the party's ideological future. And many of the winning candidates ran on platforms calling for abolishing ICE, cutting military aid to Israel and pushing for a single-payer "Medicare for All" health system. "It is undeniable that progressives have built a coalition and have a message that can serve to buoy a candidate when they are an acceptable alternative to the status quo," longtime Democratic strategist Joe Caiazzo, a veteran of progressive champion Sen. Bernie Sanders' 2016 and 2020 presidential campaigns, told Fox News Digital. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Caiazzo added, "What's incumbent upon progressives if they want to continue to be successful is to put forward candidates who are serious, credible and are accessible to the public." In Republican nominating battles, Trump took to social media late last month to tout, "My Endorsements are stronger than ever....There has never been anything close!" The numbers back up the president's assertion that despite some setbacks, he remains the ultimate kingmaker in GOP nomination showdowns. According to a Fox News Trump Primary Endorsement Tracker, the president batted a thousand in Senate GOP primaries this cycle and enjoyed a near-perfect record in House Republican nomination showdowns. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Trump has dramatically reshaped the GOP since his first White House victory a decade ago, with the populist MAGA and America First wings gaining prominence over more traditional fiscal and social conservatives. And the president's grip over party politics remains extremely firm. But he has had some setbacks, with five of his gubernatorial picks in Republican primaries this year going down to defeat. That list includes Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette, Rep. Randy Feenstra of Iowa, Wyoming Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder and Minnesota businessman and "My Pillow" founder and former CEO Mike Lindell. "The Republican Party is Trump’s party, and there’s no question that an endorsement from the president provides a tremendous boost in a Republican primary. But it doesn’t necessarily mean the candidate’s going to win," veteran GOP strategist and communicator Ryan Williams told Fox News Digital. Williams said that "the president still has a firm grip on the party, even in places where a candidate he backed loses a nomination." But he noted that "if there are underlying issues with a candidacy, those can pose problems that even an endorsement can’t overcome." After a primary season that kicked off on March 3 in Texas, North Carolina, Arkansas and Delaware bring the calendar to a close. Coons, who is running for a third full term in the Senate, is facing longshot primary challenges from University of Delaware history professor Jeff Appelhans, naval architect Mary Louve and former business executive Eric Hansen, a Republican turned Democrat. Former state Sen. Michael Katz and U.S. Army Reserves Col. John Shulli are competing for the Republican nomination. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Rep. Sarah McBride is unopposed in the Democratic primary, as she seeks a second term as Delaware's statewide House member. Republicans Joseph Arminio, Earl Cooper and John Whalen are battling for the GOP nomination. State Attorney General Kathy Jennings faces challenges for the Democratic nomination from attorney Dwayne Bensing and domestic violence victims advocate Patty Rickman. David Graham is unopposed for the GOP nomination. The Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title: MORNING GLORY: Spare us the AI apocalypse rhetoric. Let Congress decide what comes next
articles.summary: Congress and the free market should lead the debate about the future of AI not the other way around
articles.body: Every morning brings a new warning about "artificial intelligence" (AI) along the lines of, "We are all going to die." By afternoon, or by the next day at the latest, comes the counter-warning: "Stand down. Nothing to see here." For those of us who need a YouTube video to start the dishwasher or to find the emergency lights on a rental car, the correct posture is difficult to guess. "Guess" is the operative word here, because if 0.01% of America understands the debate, I would be surprised. AI EXTINCTION WARNINGS DOMINATE HEADLINES AFTER EX-ANTHROPIC EMPLOYEE'S VIRAL POST Almost everyone who cared to read or watch the Cold War unfold knew the score of that arms race when it came to nuclear weapons. Similarly, most conventional conflicts — whether Ukraine’s extraordinary defense against the Russian invasion, Israel’s multi-front war following Hamas’ Oct. 7 attack in 2023, or America’s ongoing battle with Iran to deny it both nuclear weapons and control over the Strait of Hormuz — are of the sort that most free people who want to understand those conflicts can understand (with a little time and care in choosing their sources). Not so with "AI" and its potential and dangers. RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION On Saturday, Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, said in an essay that AI was advancing too quickly for researchers to continue building it safely. Within a day, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive; Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive; and Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind’s CEO, all said they agreed on the need for a slower pace. ANTHROPIC CEO LIKENS AI FIGHT WITH CHINA TO COLD WAR, SEEKS 'DISARMAMENT NEGOTIATIONS' By Monday morning, billionaire tech investor David Sacks’ response to Amodei was everywhere on X, formerly known as Twitter, and the post had some bite. In addition to rejecting "AI doomerism," Sacks unsubtly proposed that Amodei could be motivated by self-interest (which is pretty much Adam Smith 101): "I don’t see what you see in the lab. If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible." MIKE JOHNSON REJECTS AI MORATORIUM OVER CHINA THREAT AS CONSERVATIVE ACTIVIST DEMANDS GUARDRAILS Then Sacks landed the roundhouse punch: "But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel. Stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that supersedes product liability." Sacks may or may not have President Donald Trump’s ear on this topic, but Sacks is the co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, so there is a good chance he does. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS MEETS AI AS FEARS OF HUMAN EXTINCTION JOLT CAPITOL HILL So what should President Trump do? A good answer is… nothing. If ever a possible problem had "Congress" as its final address, it is this one. There is a Senate Intelligence Committee, chaired by Arkansas Republican Sen. Tom Cotton, that has 21 members. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION There is a House Intelligence Committee, chaired by Arkansas Republican Rep. Rick Crawford, that has 27 members. These are the two committees whose membership belongs solely to the party leaders in each chamber. Those leaders tend to pick the smart folks in Congress to serve on these committees, legislators who enjoy a measure of respect on both sides of the aisle. That isn’t always the case, but generally it is true. OBAMA PRIVATELY SOUNDS ALARM ON ‘DANGEROUS’ AI, URGES DEMOCRATS TO PUT ISSUE AT CENTER OF AGENDA These 48 elected members of Congress should have the lead on this debate. It is unlikely they will have an opportunity before the midterms to gather and hear from even a half-dozen combatants in the AI wars, but the committees’ staffs can certainly be about the work of making sure the controversy is well briefed and counter-briefed. When these 48 get to hearing the arguments and debating among themselves about the best way forward — and whether that would include new statutes or a new agency with new regulatory authority over AI — they can then communicate what is advisable to communicate to the public, aware as they are, that Chinese Communist Party General Secretary Xi Jinping is watching everything we do as a country. As President Trump correctly observed about the debate over AI guardrails when it comes to China: President Xi is the guardrail. It is foolish to think Xi will be satisfied with a silver medal in the AI Olympics. TRUMP'S ANTITRUST POINT MAN COULD RESHAPE BIG TECH CASES AGAINST GOOGLE AND APPLE IF CONFIRMED We are, however, a free people, and there is no counterpart to Xi here, and we are also marked by a reluctance to trust corporate America, especially its most powerful titans, with the authority to chart our laws. As a republic of laws, it is assumed that actions by private-sector actors are legal until they can be conclusively proven not to be legal. That’s the free market. All around America is the abundance that free markets produce. When World Cup crowds dipped their collective toes in the currents of America’s vast wealth this past summer — best represented, it seemed, by Buc-ee’s — most were amazed. Americans are generally unaware of the extraordinary blessings of the combination of the rule of law and free markets. But it’s everywhere, available for everyone to see. Which means to me that Congress needs to deliberate carefully about intervening in the free market without a lot of study beforehand. The legislators can move quickly if indeed they judge the moment to be urgent. If it is urgent, I hope they do. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION But "open letters" from concerned citizens, much less self-interested CEOs, have never been the end of the discussion, and sometimes they don’t rate as beginnings or even contributions to the conversation. The future of AI is very much up to Congress. Exactly zero agencies have been established with the purpose of overseeing this technology. The Federal Trade Commission was established in 1914, so it certainly wasn’t dispatched to rule Silicon Valley and its like-minded locales. We are not organized as the European Commission is — thank goodness. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP No, the private sector gets to run with the AI ball as far and as fast as it wants until and unless Congress says stop via a proposed statute and the president agrees with a signature. That’s the final word on the debate unless and until somebody steps up with an argument based on law and not fear. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM HUGH HEWITT Hugh Hewitt is a Fox News contributor and host of "The Hugh Hewitt Show" heard weekday afternoons from 3 PM to 6 PM ET on the Salem Radio Network, and simulcast on Salem News Channel. Hugh drives Americans home on the East Coast and to lunch on the West Coast on over 400 affiliates nationwide, and on all the streaming platforms where SNC can be seen. He is a frequent guest on the Fox News Channel’s news roundtable, hosted by Bret Baier weekdays at 6pm ET. A son of Ohio and a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Michigan Law School, Hewitt has been a Professor of Law at Chapman University’s Fowler School of Law since 1996 where he teaches Constitutional Law. Hewitt launched his eponymous radio show from Los Angeles in 1990. Hewitt has frequently appeared on every major national news television network, hosted television shows for PBS and MSNBC, written for every major American paper, has authored a dozen books and moderated a score of Republican candidate debates, most recently the November 2023 Republican presidential debate in Miami and four Republican presidential debates in the 2015-16 cycle. Hewitt focuses his radio show and his column on the Constitution, national security, American politics and the Cleveland Browns and Guardians. Hewitt has interviewed tens of thousands of guests from Democrats Hillary Clinton and John Kerry to Republican Presidents George W. Bush and Donald Trump over his 40 years in broadcasting. This column previews the lead story that will drive his radio/ TV show today.

articles.title: Forget paying your ‘fair share’ of taxes. Here are 5 ways politicians want even more
articles.summary: Five ways Washington wants even more from top earners, from capital gains tax hikes and wealth taxes to estate tax changes and sneaky surtaxes.
articles.body: A few months ago, I wrote about one of my favorite phrases used by Democratic politicians in Washington, D.C.: "Pay your fair share." Politicians love saying wealthy Americans aren't paying enough. The problem is the numbers tell a different story. The top 1% of taxpayers already pay roughly 40% of federal individual income taxes. The top 10% pay the overwhelming majority of taxes. So, here's my question. If that isn't enough, what exactly is enough? BILLIONAIRE BEZOS SUGGESTS NO TAXES FOR HALF THE NATION. IS THAT CRAZY OR OVERDUE? Because the debate isn't stopping at ordinary income taxes. Soon it will be capital gains taxes, Social Security taxes and then estate taxes. Here are five more ways successful Americans could increasingly find themselves paying even more. 1. Raise your top income tax rate This is the easiest one. Need more money? Raise the top tax bracket. FORMER WASHINGTON GOVERNOR RIPS HER OWN PARTY FOR PUSHING MILLIONAIRES OUT But high earners already pay the highest federal marginal income-tax rate, plus state income taxes that can push combined marginal rates significantly higher in places like California and New York. At what percentage does "fair share" officially become fair? The last time the top tax rate was above 39.6% was 40 years ago, when it was 50%. Could it be 50% again? No political candidate will tell you that number. 2. Raise your capital gains taxes Here's another Washington favorite. This one is sneaky and likely the No. 1 tax angle to be attacked if political winds change in the White House. Tax investment gains more like ordinary income. Sounds simple until you remember where investment capital comes from. People risk money starting companies, funding businesses, buying stocks and investing in real estate because they hope to earn a return. PROGRESSIVES WANT TO TAX BILLIONAIRES FIRST, AND YOU'RE NEXT ON THE LIST You can tax that return more heavily. Just don't pretend people won't change their behavior when you do that, because they will. 3. Tax your wealth while you are living Why wait until somebody earns money? Some politicians want to tax wealth simply because someone owns it. That's a completely different ballgame. Imagine building a company worth $100 million but not having $100 million sitting in your checking account. Your business might be worth a fortune on paper while your actual cash is tied up inside the company. NEWSOM BEGS CALIFORNIANS TO VOTE 'NO' ON BILLIONAIRE'S TAX IN FACE OF MASS EXODUS, PITCHES NATIONWIDE TAX HIKE Now Uncle Sam wants a piece before you even sell it. California will tell us the first chapter of this story on the November ballot. 4. Take more when you die America already has a federal estate tax. For 2026, estates above the federal exemption can face a top estate-tax rate of 40%. Some states can take another bite. At what percentage does "fair share" officially become fair? The last time the top tax rate was above 39.6% was 40 years ago, when it was 50%. Could it be 50% again? No political candidate will tell you that number. Think about that. You earn the money. You pay income taxes. You invest what's left. And when you die, the government may want another piece of what's still sitting there. There’s a $15-million exemption today, but what if this reverts to 2000 levels, when the number was less than $1 million? Imagine your kids, your heirs and your family having to pay 50% or more to the government when you die? How many times does the same dollar need to be taxed before everybody agrees it finally paid its fair share? 5. Add another surtax This may be the sneakiest one. Don't raise the headline tax rate. Just add another little tax. There's already the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax and the additional 0.9% Medicare tax on certain higher earners. States are getting into the game as well. Massachusetts has its millionaire surtax. California has its own high-income surtax. One percent here. Four percent there. Eventually, all those "little" taxes start looking pretty big. Congress wrote the loopholes. If Congress doesn't like a provision in the tax code, change it. But don't vilify taxpayers for following the rules Congress created. That's the bigger issue with America's "fair share" debate. Maybe some taxes should go up. Maybe some deductions should disappear. Maybe certain strategies should be eliminated. We can have that debate. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION But first, politicians should answer one incredibly simple question: What exactly is fair? CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Because until somebody puts an actual number on it, "fair share" isn't tax policy. It's just two words politicians use when they want more of somebody else's money. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM TED JENKIN

articles.title: Trump’s $5,000 dividend falls flat with GOP senators
articles.summary: President Trump’s call to give all American adults $5,000 payments if Republicans win the midterm election is getting panned by Republican lawmakers, who warn they will not support giving away money to people who don’t work or pay taxes. Fiscal hawks in the GOP warn the extravagant proposal raises questions about the looming insolvency of…
articles.body:
President Trump’s call to give all American adults $5,000 payments if Republicans win the midterm election is getting panned by Republican lawmakers, who warn they will not support giving away money to people who don’t work or pay taxes.

Fiscal hawks in the GOP warn the extravagant proposal raises questions about the looming insolvency of Social Security and Medicare, which are projected to hit shortfalls in 2032 and 2033, respectively.

Trump’s proposed payments would add more than $1 trillion to the national debt and require Congress to raise the debt limit by more than initially expected to cover the reminder of his second term.

“We’re trying to figure out what that proposal is. He called it a ‘dividend’ but I don’t know what that proposal is and I’ve seen no legislation,” said Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.), who warned that pumping more than a trillion dollars into the economy could make inflation worse.

“I don’t know whether it should go out at all,” he said.

“We watched the Inflation Reduction Act and the money that was actually shipped out the door and what that did to inflation across the country,” Lankford said of the economic impact of former President Biden’s signature spending bill in 2022. “That had a detrimental effect when you throw money out.”

Other Republicans raised concern about the nation’s $40 trillion debt, which now costs more than a trillion dollars in annual interest payments.

“I haven’t seen the mechanism and mechanics around how we could get it done,” Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) said of the $5,000 dividend. “I do worry about the $40 trillion in debt that we have, and something like that would add to the national debt.”

Daines acknowledged that it was “the first time I heard it” when Trump unveiled the proposal during his primetime address at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas last Thursday.

GOP senators say they didn’t receive any heads-up from the president and don’t expect action on his proposal anytime soon.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) on Monday declined to endorse Trump’s proposal, noting the president hasn’t put out a specific plan.

“There’s no specific proposal out there and obviously how that were to come together, Congress would have a big role in determining,” he said.

Thune did suggest GOP senators wouldn’t ignore the proposal.

“There will be discussions around that subject,” he added.

But like other Republicans, Thune was blindsided by the surprise proposal.

Asked if he received any notice before Trump unveiled his $5,000 dividend proposal at last week’s GOP midterm convention, Thune said: “I did not.”

Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) said paying a dividend to Americans would make sense if the federal government were running a surplus instead of a $2 trillion annual deficit.

“Most of the time when you give out dividends, you’re running a profit. I’m thinking maybe they just forgot the negative sign. If you lose $2 trillion a year, I guess it would be a negative $5,000 dividend,” he said.

“I don’t think it would be a good idea to basically borrow money to send to the public,” he said.

“I don’t think it will come to fruition,” he added

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) said he would support putting $5,000 in funding into Americans’ retirement or investment accounts provided the money “is there.”

He said if the federal government needed to borrow them money to fund the dividend, that would be a big problem.

“If you’re telling me we’ve got to borrow the money then obviously that’s going to negatively impact people’s personal finances in the near, intermediate and long term by raising interest rates,” he said.

Other GOP lawmakers say that it would need to be reworked into a tax cut for people who pay income or payroll taxes if it is to have any chance of passage in the next Congress.

“I think we should be incentivizing work. I don’t think we should be paying people that are not working,” Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said in an interview with Fox News.

Cruz said the proposal needs to be “structured as a tax refund.”

Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine) called the idea “extraordinarily costly.”

Thune last week defended Trump’s proposal as an effort to give more money back to taxpayers, but he stopped well short of pledging to bring it to the Senate floor for a vote.

Asked if Senate Republicans would pass Trump’s $5,000 dividend, Thune replied: “Well, that’s a good question.”

“We’ll cross that bridge when we come to it,” he said.

When he was asked about whether the payout should go to people who don’t pay taxes, Thune said: “All those questions are unanswered at this point.”

Republicans are wary of embracing Trump’s plan to make large payouts to approximately 270 million Americans at a time when investors’ concerns over the national debt are driving up bond yields.

The yield on 10-year Treasurys crossed to more than 5 percent on Monday before closing for the day slightly below that mark. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has repeatedly sought to calm the bond markets, but to little avail so far.

Paul on Monday called on Congress to cut spending instead of sending out $5,000 checks to millions of Americans regardless of their employment status.

“If Washington really wanted to tackle affordability, it would rein in the reckless spending that drives inflation,” he wrote on the social platform X.

Paul is calling on Congress to adopt a budget to cut 6 cents from every dollar in federal spending across the board.

“My Six Penny Plan cuts six cents from every federal dollar spent, balancing the budget in five years and making life more affordable for everyone,” he said.

Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), who represents a state where farmers are struggling with high fuel and fertilizer prices, said Republicans need to address the affordability crisis many Americans are facing.

He said high diesel prices are a bigger issue in the Iowa gubernatorial and Senate races than the proposed $5,000 dividend. Both of those contests are competitive.

“We need to concentrate on affordability for this election. With diesel at $6 [a gallon], the best thing Trump could do is follow what a Republican president did in the ”70s and a Democrat president did in the ’70s when they were worried about the price of food: They put an embargo on soybeans and wheat,” Grassley said.

He called on Trump to stop diesel exports to reserve fuel for domestic consumption.

“He should put an embargo on diesel leaving the country because $6 diesel is a bigger issue in Iowa than $5,000,” he said, referring to the dividend.

Some Republicans, however, are applauding Trump’s dividend proposal.

Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.), who recently won a Republican primary runoff with Trump’s support, expressed support for the proposal.

Other Republican senators are on the fence.

“It kind of came as a surprise to everybody, the president’s proposal,” said Senate Republican Policy Committee Chair Shelley Moore Capito (W.Va.).

“When it’s time, we’ll take a look at it. I don’t think it will come in the immediate,” she said.

Asked about the opposition of fiscal conservatives who don’t want to send hefty payments to people who don’t work or pay taxes, Capito said: “There’s a lot of discussion, I’m sure, that’s going to be had.”

articles.title: GOP leaders throw cold water on AI regulation despite apocalyptic industry warnings
articles.summary: GOP leaders in the Capitol and White House are throwing cold water on the notion of quickly adopting new AI safeguards, despite an apocalyptic new warning from industry titans about the threat the technology poses to humankind. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) quickly dismissed the idea of moving swiftly to enact new regulations on the rapidly…
articles.body:
GOP leaders in the Capitol and White House are throwing cold water on the notion of quickly adopting new AI safeguards, despite an apocalyptic new warning from industry titans about the threat the technology poses to humankind.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) quickly dismissed the idea of moving swiftly to enact new regulations on the rapidly developing AI industry. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) on Monday didn’t reject the idea of guardrails, but he said any regulation should be done in a “light-touch way that doesn’t squash innovation.”

And President Trump, who has long rejected such guardrails, doubled down on that opposition on Monday, warning that new restrictions on American companies would merely hobble the United States amid the global AI race, while benefiting adversaries like China.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The resistance from top Republicans all but ensures the House will leave Washington this week for a seven-week, premidterm break without acting on AI legislation, despite a pounding clamor from Democrats, and some Republicans, for new limits on the technology in the wake of the industry warnings.

It also highlights the legislative limits of the current Congress, which is practically defined by partisan gridlock, heading into midterm elections where the focus — and reward — has been in attacking the other side, not bilateral cooperation.

Democrats smell blood. They’re fighting to flip control of both chambers in November, and they’re highlighting the Republicans’ opposition to new AI regulations in hopes the partisan contrast helps Democrats at the polls.

Toward that end, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) on Monday urged Republican leaders to remain in Washington to allow Congress the time to adopt tougher safety protocols for the AI companies.

Jeffries did not promote specific reforms, but he urged Congress to delay its long, preelection recess “until something is done decisively to protect the safety and the well-being of the American people.”

“Republicans have completely abandoned their responsibility to legislate and engage in public policy efforts in a responsible fashion in the area of artificial intelligence,” Jeffries said.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), meanwhile, called for a briefing for all senators about the dangers posed by AI.

“Warning bells are ringing louder than they ever have — and the Trump administration is looking the other way. Well, if they won’t hold themselves accountable, we will. And if Trump does not act, Congress must,” Schumer said in a statement Monday morning.

The topic of AI was already a campaign issue, but it was largely focused on the tangential controversy surrounding data centers, the massive facilities popping up around the country to satisfy AI’s thirst for storage and electricity.

The focus shifted sharply over the weekend, when a trio of AI trailblazers — Dario Amodei, Elon Musk and Sam Altman — stepped forward to urge a deceleration in the development of AI technology, citing the risks of global catastrophe. Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, penned a long blog post Saturday warning that a failure to tap the brakes and focus more intently on safety risks unleashing AI systems capable of orchestrating bioterrorist attacks, economic upheaval and other cataclysms.

“A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute,” Amodei wrote. He vowed that Anthropic would voluntarily slow its development and urged other companies to follow suit. Altman, who heads OpenAI, and Musk, who leads xAI, endorsed Amodei’s message.

The extraordinary warning has sparked urgent new calls from Democrats — and some Republicans — for Congress to step in immediately to adopt new guardrails that prioritize human safety.

Democratic Reps. Sam Liccardo (Calif.), George Whitesides (Calif.), Lori Trahan (Mass.) and Ted Lieu (Calif.) sent a letter to Johnson last week, urging him to have Congress “remain in session until Congress advances meaningful, bipartisan AI safeguards,” according to a copy obtained by The Hill.

“Reasonable minds may disagree about precisely how Congress should regulate this rapidly evolving technology. We cannot disagree about the imperative for Congress to act. Instead of action, you have announced vacation,” they argued, pointing to Johnson’s decision to cancel the last two weeks of the September session.

“To our children who will have read a post-apocalyptic history, ‘Why Congress Slept’” — likely written by agentic AI — our inaction will be inexplicable, and unforgivable,” they added.

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) has also called for Congress to convene a “special session,” arguing in an interview Sunday on CNN that it’s not her job and position “to hope for the best, to do nothing, and sit on my hands.” Luna said she is working with Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) on an “initial framework” to address AI concerns.

But Johnson instead has been pushing to meet with AI executives first to come up with what he says should be a “balanced approach” regarding regulation, rather than rushing into implementing guardrails. He told reporters Monday that such a meeting could take place at the end of this week or early next week, and it would include Trump.

“The reflex of legislative bodies is to cover things up with red tape and in hyperregulation. If you do that, then you lose your edge, and that is a national security concern for the American people,” Johnson said.

Thune also urged caution about rushing toward regulation, even as he acknowledged some would be necessary.

“Obviously there’s a responsibility for the companies to do that when it comes to the frontier on some of these models,” he said. “There is a way in which Congress can put guardrails around those types of more consequential threats without in any way harming our ability to stay ahead in the AI race, which I also think is very important.”

Trump went a step further, saying there’s no role for Congress at all in the AI space.

“We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Asked about whether he agrees with Trump’s social media post, Johnson said, “That’ll be part of the discussion the president has with the AI providers and all of us as we get into that meeting.”

“What the president is referring to is the necessity of maintaining our edge over our international competitors,” he continued. “I think we all can agree that’s an important thing. So we will strike the right balance, but we are not going to act irrationally or haphazardly.”

Johnson, perhaps inadvertently, touched on one of the major obstacles facing Congress as it weighs an approach to AI: The technology it would be regulating is so advanced and esoteric that it’s unclear whether most lawmakers can grasp the changes they’d be voting on.

There’s also the question of how effective new regulations would be if they governed only American AI companies. Some experts stress the importance of securing a global pact encompassing all the world’s AI giants, wherever they are.

Members of Congress have introduced dozens of bills addressing artificial intelligence, but action has yet to be taken on these measures. Last week, Reps. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) and Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.) introduced the bipartisan Stop Rogue AI Act, aimed at ensuring businesses and federal agencies can spot and stop dangerous AI agents operating within their networks. In July, Reps. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) and Lieu introduced the AI Kill Switch Act, requiring AI system developers to “maintain the technical capability to throttle, suspend, or shut them down.”

articles.title: Ken Paxton’s plight in Texas is mostly of his own making
articles.summary: The saying goes that victory has a thousand fathers but defeat is an orphan. That doesn’t mean, however, that there won’t be any paternity claims after a loss. And if Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) really does manage to lose his Senate race against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, naming the father of what…
articles.body:
The saying goes that victory has a thousand fathers but defeat is an orphan. That doesn’t mean, however, that there won’t be any paternity claims after a loss.

And if Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) really does manage to lose his Senate race against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, naming the father of what would be an epochal defeat for Texas Republicans will be a Maury Povich-level meltdown.

The most obvious culprit would be Paxton himself, who, in addition to assembling a highly polarizing record during his 23 years in public office, has dragged forward enough baggage from his personal and professional life to fill the cargo hold of the Titanic.

We know that in the “attention economy” era, divisive positions and personal scandals don’t have to be career killers in politics — see Trump, Donald J. But it takes a lot of charisma and showmanship to pull that off. Paxton, on the other hand, brings the verve and energy of a coroner’s inquest to the campaign trail.

The next most obvious person to blame would be the man who Paxton beat in the Republican primary, Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas).

After 41 years in a political career that, going all the way back to his time as a circuit judge in San Antonio, has been marked by decorous restraint, Cornyn is very obviously enjoying letting it rip on Paxton.

After warning Republicans what a risk they would be taking with his longtime foe, Cornyn seems to be enjoying his I-told-you-so moment. There’s something to the charge. Had the two rivals made peace and Cornyn was out stumping for Paxton, assuring traditional conservatives and squishy suburbanites that he was vouching for the attorney general, it would do some good.

Where the Cornyn charge loses steam, though, is that Paxton, typically proud and defiant, probably wasn’t asking for Cornyn’s blessing. And Paxton was already a universally known figure to Texas voters before Cornyn started calling him out.

Paxton set the record in 2018 for the worst performance by a Republican seeking statewide office in Texas this century. (Former Gov. Rick Perry got a lower share of the vote in 2006 than Paxton did in 2018, but that was a wild four-way contest that featured two independent candidates, including musician Kinky Friedman. Perry still won by 10 points.)

For statewide Republican candidates in the era of ruby-red Texas, Paxton was the pits even before his impeachment and plea deal . Voters didn’t need Cornyn to tell them that.

It’s also true that Talarico’s primary opponent, Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), is out there briefing against the Democratic nominee. So if Cornyn is a liability for Paxton, it is of a kind that both candidates and parties share equally.

There’s another obvious person to blame if Paxton does go down: President Trump himself.

In the larger sense, this is clearly true. Paxton would be disadvantaged with any Republican in the White House given voters’ longstanding preference for divided government and its manifestation in the midterm curse.

Trump is also specifically a target for blame because the policies he has pursued have helped drive the cost of a gallon of diesel fuel in petroleum-rich Texas to nearly $6.

Trump’s proposed balm for the anger of working-class voters irritated by that is for the government to borrow huge sums of money and give it away, which, in turn irritates the more affluent, more conservative Cornyn voters who already didn’t like Paxton.

But the charge against Trump doesn’t withstand close scrutiny.

It is true that Trump’s job approval in Texas is pretty scrawny for a state he won by 14 points two years ago, but it’s also true that Trump is at about break-even. He may be a couple of points underwater in Texas but it’s not nearly as bad as it in in places like Georgia , where anti-Trump sentiment is swamping Republican candidates.

If they re-ran the 2024 presidential election in Texas today, Trump might not beat former Vice President Kamala Harris by 14 points again, but he’d almost certainly still prevail.

Nor can you say that Trump isn’t doing enough to help.

Trump’s big GOP hootenanny in Dallas last week was basically a telethon for Paxton. Trump told his supporters, essentially, that Paxton is such a schlub that Republicans need to dig deep to help him win.

Democrats snickered at Trump’s put-downs of Paxton, but the session undoubtedly was a boost for the beleaguered candidate. He got a massive cash infusion and a new persona from Trump as a kind of pitiful figure, which is an improvement over his conventional image as calculating and aloof.

Whether he wins or loses, Paxton really seems likely to break his own 2018 record when he squeaked by his reelection with 50.6 percent of the vote. There’s a Libertarian candidate in the race who will soak up a number of votes from fed-up conservatives, so Paxton’s best-case scenario right now looks like a narrow plurality win .

But Paxton’s title as the worst-performing statewide Texas Republican will probably still fall, anyway.

The Texas GOP nominated Bo French to be the state’s next railroad commissioner, serving on the three-member board that regulates the state’s energy industry. French knocked off incumbent Republican Commissioner Jim Wright in the GOP primary and was bound for an easy win for an office that is almost always decided by partisan affiliation.

But on Saturday, French apparently became incensed by images online of what appeared to be University of Texas students of South Asian ancestry celebrating the Longhorns’ comeback win over Ohio State.

French’s outrage over what the original post called “Bollywood University” did not fade with the cold light of morning, either. He stayed on the social media rampage, saying of Cornyn and other Republicans who condemned French’s disdain for the non-white Texas students “America Last losers are mad that Texas Republicans are starting to put America First.”

Paxton was careful not to specifically condemn French’s behavior, saying something about how racism was bad generally but what he said was Talarico’s problem with “whiteness.” Ooof.

So, if Paxton does lose, he will mostly have himself to blame, but he can throw in a little something extra for Mr. French.

articles.title: Why Donald Trump has a Joe Biden problem
articles.summary: During the 2024 presidential campaign, President Trump repeatedly slammed then-President Biden for not understanding the economic pain Americans were feeling. In rallies and speeches, Trump made the case that Biden and his small circle of aides were touting jobs numbers and low unemployment but were still out of touch with the rising cost of groceries,…
articles.body:
During the 2024 presidential campaign, President Trump repeatedly slammed then-President Biden for not understanding the economic pain Americans were feeling.

In rallies and speeches, Trump made the case that Biden and his small circle of aides were touting jobs numbers and low unemployment but were still out of touch with the rising cost of groceries, housing and other expenses.

Now, with just 49 days left until the midterm elections, some Republicans worry Trump is confronting the same kind of economic disconnect that plagued his predecessor.

“Trump has a Biden problem,” one of the president’s former campaign aides told The Hill. “He’s basically saying, ‘Look at the numbers; you’re wrong in how you feel.’ That’s the same exact thing Biden was saying, and that’s why we won.”

The war in Iran, which began in February, has caused gas prices to rise rapidly, while airfare, travel and shipping have soared.

Tariffs have also contributed to higher prices on consumer goods. Inflation, which stood at 2.7 percent at the end of 2025, was 3.4 percent in August, according to a Friday report by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Those figures could also create a headache for Republicans heading into November.

Trump has repeatedly blamed a bad economy he inherited from Biden for any bad economic news while touting good news about the economy, including low unemployment.

But many Americans aren’t feeling the good economic vibes as they struggle to pay their rent or mortgages or fill up their cars. And the Trump messaging, like the Biden messaging when the Democrat was in the White House, is falling flat.

Kevin Madden, a Republican strategist who worked as a senior adviser on Mitt Romney’s presidential campaign in 2012, agreed there is a parallel, saying there’s “a fundamental question at the heart of the average voter’s assessment of the president” and the broader system in Washington, and that is, “Do they understand what I’m going through?”

“In 2024, Biden was underwater with voters largely because he seemed out of touch with both the causes and the solutions related to the issue of inflation,” Madden said. “For too long, he claimed it was temporary, and then he took too long to provide any real solutions to address the pain the issue was causing.”

“Fast forward to 2026, and members of Congress are returning to their states and districts and hearing a similar refrain about the cost of living,” Madden added. “Voters need to know that Washington gets it and is doing something about it.”

In recent weeks, the president has sought to persuade Americans he understands their frustration — while arguing the higher costs stemming from war are necessary.

“Ultimately, prices are going to come down. … Will it happen before the election? I can’t tell you that, but I think people are very smart,” Trump said late last month, answering a question from a reporter on the elevated prices. “They know we had to go into Iran. It only went up because of Iran.”

Polling underscores voter dissatisfaction with the economy and the Trump administration’s handling of economic affairs.

A Quinnipiac University poll released last week showed 32 percent of registered voters approved of Trump’s handling of the economy, while 65 percent disapproved.

Among independent voters, the numbers were even starker, with 21 percent approving of Trump’s handling of the economy and 75 percent disapproving.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll out at the end of August showed 22 percent of those surveyed said they approved of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, while 71 percent disapproved.

The same survey also revealed 47 percent of registered voters said the cost of living would be the most important factor in deciding their vote in November’s midterms.

Republicans say the poll numbers underscore the difficult path ahead in trying to convince voters about their economic anxieties, particularly as they see the war in Iran drag on and gas prices jump by the day.

“Trump’s challenge, much like Biden, is that it’s hard to tell people what they feel is wrong,” Republican strategist Doug Heye said.

Democrats acknowledge there are parallels between Biden’s and Trump’s insistence that voters would come around. But they say that unlike Republicans on Biden, Democrats have a better story to tell on Trump because his direct actions on Iran and tariffs caused a shaky economy.

“The macro is the same, but what’s very different is that Trump is actively doing things that are making people’s lives worse,” one Democratic strategist said. “The public can make the connection on Trump’s meddling in the economy, which is making things more expensive.”

Susan Del Percio, a longtime Republican strategist who does not support Trump, warned that Trump’s approach on the economy may not be effective.

“Trump is basically saying to voters, ‘Get over it. Man up. And believe me because I’m always right,’” Del Percio said. “Well, voters aren’t seeing that anymore.”

While other Republicans acknowledge Trump may change course depending on the results of the midterms, Del Percio said she has her doubts.

“If Republicans lost the House and Senate, he’s not going to change,” she said. “He believes in what he’s saying. He is in that bubble. And it’s not even being disconnected. He’s just living in the land of Trump.”

articles.title: Voters have a blunt message for Trump about his idea to dole out $5,000 checks
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's $5,000 dividend check proposal drew sharp reactions from voters, with some calling it a publicity stunt unlikely to pass Congress.
articles.body: Voters aren't convinced that President Donald Trump will make good on his new promise to send eligible Americans $5,000 dividend checks if Republicans maintain their majorities in the House and Senate this midterm cycle. The proposal, which Trump unveiled during the Republican National Committee's midterm convention in Dallas last week, has ignited a national debate over whether the payments are financially feasible — and whether they'll ever become reality. Asked what they thought of the proposal, and whether they believed it would ever become reality, most voters were skeptical, with several dismissing the idea as unrealistic while pointing to Congress, the nation's debt and previous promises they said never materialized. A few were hopeful. "Personally, I think it's just a publicity stunt and I don't think that it's ever gonna happen," a voter named William said when speaking with Fox News Digital. "It'll need to go through Congress, and I don't think with the midterm elections... the possibility of that happening is just so far down the road." TRUMP'S $5,000 DIVIDEND CHECKS WOULD COME WITH A MAJOR CATCH UNDER GOP SENATOR'S PLAN As Fox News Digital previously reported, the dividend proposal would require congressional approval, and it's unclear where the money would come from to fund the program. Another voter was clued into the dilemma and questioned whether the federal government, under it's 40.1 trillion in national debt, could afford the proposal. "I don't think we have the money for that," said Daniel from Maryland. "And I think if we did, it should be going a couple different other places than that for sure." Liz from Alexandria, Virginia, was even more blunt, calling the idea "absolute nonsense." "I don't believe a word that man ever says," she added in reference to Trump. Another cited previous promises they believed had fallen short. "Last time I remember he promised a stimulus and a couple other things. None of that happened," the voter said. The president argued the checks would be funded through tariff revenue — but with an estimated price tag of roughly $1.2 trillion, the total needed far exceeds the record customs duties the federal government has collected under Trump's tariff agenda. articles.title: Trump’s data center push fractures Congress as local anger explodes: 'Grasping at straws'
articles.summary: Democratic lawmakers push to restrict data centers over water use and electricity bills while Republicans highlight AI race benefits and local control.
articles.body: Democratic lawmakers are calling for tighter restrictions on data centers, while Republicans say the facilities could boost the economy and keep the U.S. ahead in the artificial intelligence (AI) race. President Donald Trump doubled down on data centers this week, rejecting calls to slow development after previously warning that communities blocking the facilities would "end up being backwards and poor." Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., told Fox News Digital last month that Arizona needs to slow the expansion of data centers until the state fully assesses its long-term impacts. "We in Arizona need to pause the expansion of data centers in the state until we really figure out a plan on how we're going to preserve our water, how we are going to make sure that ratepayers aren't taking on the responsibility," Ansari said. MAGA BEGINS TO CRACK AS 2026 GOP ROSTER BACKS AWAY FROM TRUMP'S TECH VISION Ansari called President Trump's support for data centers "out of touch," saying it runs counter to what the "vast majority" of Americans want. "If Donald Trump is such a big fan of data centers, then he should welcome them in his own backyard," she said. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., pointed to his proposed Data Center Bill of Rights, which would ban data centers within 2,500 feet of homes, schools, childcare facilities, hospitals and nursing homes and give communities greater authority over where they're built. Khanna dismissed President Donald Trump's comments that communities opposing data centers would fall behind. "Trump has failed to deliver for the forgotten American, so he's just grasping at straws," he said. Rep. Jonathan Jackson, D-Ill., said lawmakers must prioritize what's "fair" for local communities. "The wealth has gone into the tech sector, and they are unregulated, unbridled and not very philanthropic," Jackson said. WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE Higher electricity bills shouldn't fall on communities as data centers expand, according to Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich. "It baffles me that we are just not guaranteeing, for average ratepayers, low utility bills," she said. "These data centers could play a role in that." Republican lawmakers were split on data centers, with some saying they can boost economies and others stressing local control. Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., backed AI investment to compete with China but opposed building data centers in residential neighborhoods. "We've got to stay ahead of China with AI, and data centers are a part of that," Mace said. "But you don't put them in somebody's backyard and that's the whole point." Praising data centers, Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., said they can generate tax revenue, improve local infrastructure and support energy production. CRACKDOWN ON CRITICAL TECH COULD OPEN AMERICANS TO A NEW NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT "You should be fighting over them," McCormick said. "But, I mean, if you don't want one, that's up to you. I think you're missing out." Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., said decisions about data centers should be left to states and local communities. "I believe in 10th Amendment rights, state rights," Norman said. "Let each community take ownership, and they'll make the right decisions."
