articles.title: Christiana Stephenson: Communications director, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY)
articles.summary: Christiana Stephenson has spent more than seven years helping House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) navigate the relentless communications demands of House Democratic leadership. Stephenson joined Jeffries’s leadership operation as press secretary in January 2019, when he was House Democratic Caucus chair. She has been with him ever since. Her path to the Capitol was less direct. Stephenson first…
articles.body:
Christiana Stephenson has spent more than seven years helping House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) navigate the relentless communications demands of House Democratic leadership.

Stephenson joined Jeffries’s leadership operation as press secretary in January 2019, when he was House Democratic Caucus chair. She has been with him ever since.

Her path to the Capitol was less direct.

Stephenson first interned on Capitol Hill in 2010 for Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), an experience she said convinced her she wanted to return. But she was rejected for a series of staff assistant and legislative correspondent jobs before a friend helped her land a position at a public relations agency — an opportunity that ultimately steered her toward communications.

“It took a few years to get there, but walking into the Capitol every day really does feel like a full circle moment,” she said.

Now, as communications director, Stephenson is one of the senior aides responsible for helping shape and communicate Jeffries’ message, while also responding to the latest congressional firestorms.

“It’s cliche, but no two days are the same,” Stephenson said, describing the most interesting part of the job. “I love the daily opportunities to throw myself into something new. I wish there were more hours in the day to be able to serve the Leader, our Members and to spend time with my own team.”

One assignment stands out above the rest.

In 2024, Stephenson accompanied Jeffries on a bipartisan codel to Normandy marking the 80th anniversary of D-Day. Six months pregnant at the time, she met veterans who had participated in the invasion — an experience she described as both “humbling and meaningful.”

She plans to someday show her daughter the photographs from the trip and tell her about the heroes they met.

Her role has also evolved alongside her family. She said she has gone from being an “office rat” who could travel at a moment’s notice to a working mother balancing the demands of leadership communications with multiple children at home.

She acknowledges she has no perfect formula for handling the pressure of Capitol Hill. She noted that she is “as addicted” to her phone and doomscrolling “as anyone else.” But after years in the job, she said, perspective helps.

Some of the most stressful moments, she said, have eventually become memories she looks back on with “pride and amusement.”

articles.body:
Advancing any legislation with a slim Republican majority is a challenge, but navigating the variety of GOP viewpoints while trying to advance appropriations bills adds a new layer of difficulty.

For Marcus Towns, the member services director for the House Appropriations Committee, it helps to be a people person.

“It’s a very personality-driven job,” Towns said. “My main focus is getting things out of committee and working with our staff to do that.”

Towns ensures members’ opinions are heard and considered — his job essentially is to keep all the committee Republicans happy enough to vote for all 12 appropriations bills.

“It can be little things like we set up food during markups and just make sure that they’re fed and all happy and not super angry about these long days, because they’re here for 12 to 16 hours back-to-back days sometimes,” Towns said.

In dealing with dueling Republican factions, Towns said it helps to remind himself that everyone is human.

“At the end of the day, it’s dealing with other peoples’ parents and grandparents. So sometimes they’re in a bad mood, but it might not be related to anything that’s work-related,” Towns said. “Are they going to be team players that day? A lot of times, sometimes people just need a break.”

Towns started his political career working on state and federal campaigns in Illinois, before relocating to D.C. for what he thought would be a short-term internship with the House Ways and Means Committee.

“I came here and didn’t think I was going to last, and now I’ve been here for five years,” Towns said.

Prior to joining the Appropriations Committee, Towns worked as member services director for the House Foreign Affairs Committee, which is where he said he learned the importance of consensus building.

“You have to give people wins everywhere, and so one of the main goals [of then-Chair Michael McCaul (R-Texas)] was, ‘I want every one of my members to have a bill out of committee,’” Towns said. “That’s how I learned to do this job.”

articles.title: Raphaël Schreiber: Legislative director, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.)
articles.summary: July 15, 2025, was “the most stressful day” of Raphaël Schreiber’s career in Congress. The legislative director for Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) had a “very brief” conversation with the congressman about the idea of a bill directing the Department of Justice to publicly release materials on its Jeffrey Epstein investigation. “And then he told me,…
articles.body:
July 15, 2025, was “the most stressful day” of Raphaël Schreiber’s career in Congress.

The legislative director for Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) had a “very brief” conversation with the congressman about the idea of a bill directing the Department of Justice to publicly release materials on its Jeffrey Epstein investigation.

“And then he told me, ‘You have until the end of the day to get it done,’” Schreiber said — a far cry from the weeks of bill writing that is typical and a turnaround he’d never seen in a personal office before.

After a whirlwind day of drafting, consulting with lawyers to make sure the ultimate product could survive a court challenge, working with parliamentarians in Congress on procedure, and teaming up with Rep. Ro Khanna’s (D-Calif.) staff, the Epstein Files Transparency Act and an accompanying discharge petition to force a vote got filed by that evening.

The bill ended up being one of the most politically consequential pieces of legislation of President Trump’s second term. The White House for months furiously lobbied against it. Around a dozen Republicans had co-sponsored the resolution to tee up the bill, but only three other Republicans — Rep. Nancy Mace (S.C.), Rep. Lauren Boebert (Colo.), and then-Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (Ga.) — signed on to the discharge petition.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) critiqued the way the bill was written, arguing that it did not adequately protect victims of Epstein’s abuse.

“It’s something when the third-most powerful person in the country is commenting on your work directly,” Schreiber said. “I had a heart attack the first time I heard it — thinking, ‘Crap, did I mess up something?’”

“Obviously, when you read the language, there was more than ample language for the protection of the victims. The victims’ lawyers had affirmed this,” Schreiber said. “And three judges also affirmed it, two in the Southern District of New York and one in the Southern District of Florida, attesting to the very clear, plain language of the bill.”

Unable to sway the three Republican women and facing a floor vote on the bill, Trump at the last minute threw his support behind the Epstein Files Transparency Act and signed it.

Schreiber’s advice to other legislative staffers is not to wait until being handed an assignment to get busy: “If you have time on your hands, study something new and apply it.”

articles.title: Jessica Hayes: Senior adviser in district, Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.)
articles.summary: Jessica Hayes said serving in Georgia’s 10th Congressional District during the chaotic and deadly U.S. evacuation of Afghanistan in August 2021 was a “holy calling.” Now a senior adviser working in the 9th District for Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.), Hayes was working for former Rep. Jody Hice (R-Ga.) when the office started getting calls from…
articles.body:
Jessica Hayes said serving in Georgia’s 10th Congressional District during the chaotic and deadly U.S. evacuation of Afghanistan in August 2021 was a “holy calling.”

Now a senior adviser working in the 9th District for Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.), Hayes was working for former Rep. Jody Hice (R-Ga.) when the office started getting calls from panicked people trying to help their loved ones get out of Afghanistan as the U.S. left and the Taliban took over.

The caseload quickly ballooned from constituents to calls from people all over the country and world, desperate to find a U.S. official who could help get family or friends at risk from the Taliban out of the country.

Hayes described herself and other district staff as having “this special calling.”

Far away from Washington, D.C., they don’t always get the same recognition as staff in the Capitol working on policy — but they are in many ways on the front lines of serving constituents.

“We’re there to really work on behalf of so many constituents who are in need. They [district staff] don’t get a lot of praise, they don’t get a lot of pay, they just kind of keep their head down and their hand to the grindstone, and they do this day in and day out.”

Hayes described it as a miracle that she was even in Hice’s office in 2021. A year earlier, he had approached her about running for Congress, which she declined after weighing the effects on her family.

During the fraught, 24/7 work of trying to evacuate people, Hayes realized that if she had decided to run for Congress, she wouldn’t be in the trenches helping Americans and America’s allies. In a letter from the Nazarene Fund, which helped with the evacuations, Hice and his staff were thanked for helping 12,500 people get out of the country, including U.S. citizens and permanent residents, American war allies, persecuted Christians, at-risk women and judges and lawyers.

Hice praised Hayes for her unique ability to earn love and respect among staff, while also challenging them and pushing for excellence.

He said staff members describe her as the type of person who will walk with her arm over your shoulder in encouragement, while also kicking you in the back of the pants as motivation.

“She’s just one of those folks that has a unique capacity to accomplish that,” he said.

articles.title: Alyssa Erdel: Deputy chief of staff, House Republican Conference
articles.summary: Heading up member services is a “chameleon position,” Alyssa Erdel says — highly adaptable depending on the vision of the lawmaker in charge, whether for the House’s Republican Conference or in a committee. “My mission is always the same: I listen, identify what’s missing, build trusted relationships, solve problems, and fill voids,” Erdel said. Erdel…
articles.body:
Heading up member services is a “chameleon position,” Alyssa Erdel says — highly adaptable depending on the vision of the lawmaker in charge, whether for the House’s Republican Conference or in a committee.

“My mission is always the same: I listen, identify what’s missing, build trusted relationships, solve problems, and fill voids,” Erdel said.

Erdel still does that — and more — as deputy chief of staff for the House Republican Conference under Chairwoman Lisa McClain (R-Mich.).

Erdel said her new role includes managing the communications team, leading meetings and working with McClain on management and strategy to execute her vision, as well as the member services leadership position she previously held.

Leading member services for the GOP conference means that Erdel talks to a lot of staff across the conference to help figure out what they need. Then she helps them make connections, aids in education for members and other staff, and fills any gaps in lawmakers’ operation of their offices.

One recent project of the House GOP conference was launching a “Meet the Cabinet” series, giving House Republicans the opportunity to meet members of President Trump’s Cabinet, enabling them to build relationships and make any specific requests.

Connecting the staff members at the committee level or Trump administration level is as important as connecting the principals, Erdel said.

“It’s not about where they stand ideologically. It’s about what their need is,” Erdel said, giving an example: “Are they in need of an Appropriations 101, or is their staff?”

The House GOP also launched a communications director mentorship program, has a scheduler mentorship program, and provides training for staff members.

“It’s like arming the entire conference, giving them the tools to be successful,” Erdel said.

Each of the 219 House Republican members, and their offices, have different needs. For veteran members with a stable staff, Erdel can connect with their staffers directly; other members might want to communicate on a more personal level.

McClain’s vision, Erdel said, is to “lift up” every member of the House GOP, be it through helping them advocate for their priorities with the Trump administration; helping them get national media attention; helping them solve constituent issues; or providing opportunities to learn about intricate policy issues.

The key, she said, is “knowing the members, knowing their districts, knowing their staff, understanding their constituencies.”

“And most importantly: Consistent execution, so when you’re hearing of something, you’re not just the eyes and ears — you are consistently executing and making this place just run a little bit smoother and be a little bit stronger,” Erdel said.

articles.title: Andrew Bower: Deputy staff director, House Oversight Committee Democrats
articles.summary: Andrew Bower followed Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) from his personal office to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee as Democrats elevated a fresh face, and with him, a fresh new approach to investigations. The committee has faced an avalanche of issues, but it’s the probe into deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein that Bower said “has…
articles.body:
Andrew Bower followed Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) from his personal office to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee as Democrats elevated a fresh face, and with him, a fresh new approach to investigations.

The committee has faced an avalanche of issues, but it’s the probe into deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein that Bower said “has really defined the committee’s arc and vision.”

“There’s so much pressure from the survivor communities to whom we owe so much, and from the American people who are watching all of this, that it’s owed an enormous amount of time and resources, and it deserves it,” Bower, 33, told The Hill.

However, he acknowledged, “Any investigation where we’re going to be deposing former presidents and Cabinet secretaries … has the risk of blocking out the sun.”

As deputy staff director, Bower has been a big part of rethinking the panel’s goals under President Trump and weighing how to balance its broad investigative reach with what might resonate most with the public.

Bower said in some cases, that’s meant a shift to trying to take information already in the public sphere and make it more digestible.

“We can uncover a contract that shouldn’t have been awarded, or a payment. … But in full view, [Trump’s] made $2 billion off of crypto. It is a real balance,” Bower said, adding that the guiding principle is that Americans have a right to know what their government is doing.

“It’s our job to uncover the facts that help them understand what that is. On the other hand, sometimes what we are doing is organizing public facts in a way that the American people can understand — I’m calling attention to lights that are flashing right in front of us.”

The committee credits Bower with being behind a few of its viral moments. Though Bower’s TV preferences skew more toward “The Simpsons” than “The Real Housewives,” knowing his boss was a fan he intertwined a moment from the franchise’s Salt Lake City show into a line of questioning.

He advises newer staffers that they should be “as deeply embedded in Twitter as you can psychologically tolerate, unfortunately.”

“Obviously Twitter is not real life, but lots of members think it’s real life,” he said, adding that it’s important to see what members are looking at as well as discourse on the other side.

Sometimes those fights, he said, are what “drives the House floor and political dynamics … especially in a very narrow minority where very online members can wield an insane amount of power.”

articles.title: Zach Barnes: Executive director, House Freedom Caucus
articles.summary: Zach Barnes says that working with members of the House Freedom Caucus — the hard-line conservative group famous for confronting Republican leadership and instigating procedural and floor fights — makes him joke about how Congress must have operated a century ago. “Members of Congress didn’t have 15 to 18 full-time staff in D.C., in their…
articles.body:
Zach Barnes says that working with members of the House Freedom Caucus — the hard-line conservative group famous for confronting Republican leadership and instigating procedural and floor fights — makes him joke about how Congress must have operated a century ago.

“Members of Congress didn’t have 15 to 18 full-time staff in D.C., in their districts. They had maybe one administrative assistant,” Barnes said. “A lot of the Freedom Caucus members are sharp, know the procedure, spend a lot of time working on it. I think they’d be just as effective 100 years ago as they are now.”

Not only do many of the group’s members know and talk to the House parliamentarian, they also have deep knowledge of policy and talk to subject matter experts themselves.

That dynamic means Barnes isn’t so much guiding the group as its executive director, but rather ensuring its members have everything necessary to execute their plan.

“It’s incumbent upon me that I’ve got to overperform, and I’ve got to work with all their staffs and make sure we’re all overperforming,” Barnes said.

He follows up with leadership staff and committee staff, makes sure he has not only the top line from a meeting but also supporting material, and makes that information usable for all the members of the caucus — all in hopes of advancing shared goals for Republicans as a whole.

This year, one of the biggest policy fights for the House Freedom Caucus has been over reauthorization of foreign spy powers under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), with members pushing for reforms to better protect Americans’ privacy. Barnes was integral to the caucus spearheading that FISA push.

The Freedom Caucus members eventually got the White House and House Republican leadership to abandon their push for a “clean” reauthorization without reforms. The House passed a compromise, but the fight led to FISA lapsing for the first time ever. Freedom Caucus members note, though, that current certifications authorized by the FISA court continue into next year.

“They’re able to take a sober look. They’re able to point their colleagues toward the facts of the law. The members’ goal is to balance the national security priorities with protecting the privacy rights of Americans,” Barnes said. “My job is to help them organize, help them take the hill, make sure everybody’s operating off of the facts of the law.”

articles.title: Julia Bartusek: Executive director, House Democratic Women’s Caucus
articles.summary: Julia Bartusek never expected to end up in Washington. The executive director of the House Democratic Women’s Caucus grew up on a pig farm in Minnesota, a far cry from the halls of Congress where she now helps shape one of the House Democrats’ most prominent coalitions. But she said that she’s always had an…
articles.body:
Julia Bartusek never expected to end up in Washington.

The executive director of the House Democratic Women’s Caucus grew up on a pig farm in Minnesota, a far cry from the halls of Congress where she now helps shape one of the House Democrats’ most prominent coalitions.

But she said that she’s always had an interest in women’s issues.

“When you learn about the gender pay gap for the first time, you’re like, ‘What the heck is going on?’” Bartusek recalled.

She joined the caucus three years ago as its first policy director and eventually became executive director, overseeing the group’s strategy, staff and relationships with its members. During her tenure, she said, the caucus has grown not only in membership but also in influence and visibility — including a jump in its Instagram following from roughly 3,000 to nearly 85,000.

But Bartusek’s job extends well beyond traditional women’s issues. The caucus has pushed into debates over WNBA labor negotiations, immigration and the treatment of women in Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention, and efforts involving survivors of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

That work has produced some of the moments Bartusek said she will remember most.

During President Trump’s State of the Union address in February, she helped escort Epstein survivors to their seats as Democrats sought to keep attention on their stories.

“I feel fortunate that they’ve trusted us with their stories,” she said.

Her work can also be emotionally heavy. Bartusek has played a leading role in bipartisan negotiations over sexual misconduct reform on Capitol Hill, an issue she said carries particular weight as a woman working on the Hill herself.

“The hardest part of this job is just how real the issues are. And I think that you know, a lot of Hill staff sometimes don’t get to acknowledge the actual human emotional toll that working on some of these issues can have,” she said.

As Bartusek looks toward the possibility of Democrats returning to the House majority, she expects the caucus to push aggressively on reproductive health, including abortion access, contraception and in vitro fertilization, while continuing its work on economic costs, healthcare and women’s safety.

“They don’t feel represented by the current government. They feel like their vote is at risk and they feel like their lives are at risk. And so we’ll always show up and respond to that, whether they’re in a red district or a blue district,” she said.

articles.title: Chris Bien: Deputy chief of staff, Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.)
articles.summary: Managing the House floor is a big job in any Speaker’s office. That challenge is turned up to the max in the current House Republican majority, where super-slim margins and a culture of rebellion make drama on the House floor a regular occurrence. Chris Bien, Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) deputy chief of staff, has helped…
articles.body:
Managing the House floor is a big job in any Speaker’s office. That challenge is turned up to the max in the current House Republican majority, where super-slim margins and a culture of rebellion make drama on the House floor a regular occurrence.

Chris Bien, Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) deputy chief of staff, has helped the GOP majority deal with that uncertainty and defy the odds to deliver under pressure.

“Our job is to know the rules and procedures of the institution and how we want to execute what we want to do as the majority — how do we advance not only the Speaker’s priorities, but our members’ priorities and the administration’s priorities together?” Bien said.

In June, Bien was promoted from floor director to deputy chief of staff in the Speaker’s office — retaining his leadership over a team of six in floor operations while taking on other responsibilities to assist the chief of staff.

An intraparty dispute making it to the House floor sometimes means making a call to pull a vote or let it fail. Other times, it means holding a vote open while lawmakers negotiate to get enough Republicans to “yes.”

“It’s a little bit of art. There’s no magic formula,” Bien said. “Hopefully, we were able to do a lot of the legwork before and sort of sniff out a lot of those issues. We rely on the leader’s team, the whip team too, to help give us information, give us context to where these members are.”

In this Congress, Bien has helped Republicans usher through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and overcome countless stalled procedural votes. He spoke with The Hill the week that House Republicans passed a flurry of major legislation before leaving for August recess.

It is of paramount importance to have trust with not only the members of staff of one’s own party, but also across the aisle, Bien said, so that the floor staff can have free flow of information and anticipate what might happen.

“At the end of the day, members want to be productive, get stuff done. They want to be able to be part of the solution to figuring things out. And so it’s just making sure to hear them out, understand where they’re coming from, and making sure that we can advocate for what they think is important,” Bien said.

articles.title: Rubi Flores: Policy director, Congressional Hispanic Caucus
articles.summary: Rubi Flores, 30, is a concert pianist turned policy director who has landed at the Congressional Hispanic Caucus (CHC) as it positions itself to fight the Trump administration on its mass deportation agenda and other issues key to Latinos. An immigrant from Mexico who moved to the U.S. at age 10, Flores excelled not only…
articles.body:
Rubi Flores, 30, is a concert pianist turned policy director who has landed at the Congressional Hispanic Caucus (CHC) as it positions itself to fight the Trump administration on its mass deportation agenda and other issues key to Latinos.

An immigrant from Mexico who moved to the U.S. at age 10, Flores excelled not only at piano but at cello as well and aimed to make music her career. But as she advanced to college, some of the most competitive conservatories remained out of reach financially.

“It was one of the first times that the world told me no, and that made me evaluate, what are the circumstances to led me to not be able to have that dream?” she told The Hill. That question led to “opening up a lot of conversations in my mind of the inequities worldwide.”

“Undergrad, leadership positions, and things like this really make you think that, ‘Oh, I can change the world.’ And I wanted to change the world; I wanted to make it a little bit better,” she said.

College was also where Flores began to first engage in activism, and she set about achieving new dreams.

After a stint as a Fulbright scholar in Mexico, Flores interned at Fwd.us, where she tracked asylum policy across the globe. From there, she went to work on the Biden campaign as chief of staff to campaign manager Julie Chávez.

Now at the CHC, Flores said the group is evaluating how to best play to its strengths while in the minority, a role that has involved being an active voice in pushing back on President Trump’s immigration agenda, visiting detention centers and highlighting conditions, and filing amicus briefs in a bevy of litigation now before the courts.

Flores said being both an immigrant and a trans woman are crucial lenses for how she approaches her work, including how the party can protect both groups in an age where a larger share of Latinos than ever before backed the GOP when they voted for Trump.

On both issues, Flores said, “That’s my overall goal to make sure that we have positions that are winnable while staying true to our values and our efforts,” adding that programming for the caucus has discussed how to “inoculate themselves from a lot of attacks on from the right, and also how to just have an agenda that, while remaining popular, can defend the community.”

articles.title: Washington’s AI response falls into predictable patterns: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, our reporters dig into how Washington is — and isn’t — responding to the latest warnings about the threats of AI. Plus, senior national politics reporter Natasha Korecki examines some early signs of the 2028 presidential campaign sticking out in the thick of the midterm elections. — Scott Bland Washington’s response to AI warnings has fallen into predictable patterns so far This week’s big warnings about the risks of artificial intelligence didn’t come out of nowhere. In September 2023, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and other billionaire tech titans huddled with senators in the Capitol to discuss what Musk called the “civilizational risk” posed by artificial intelligence, NBC News’ Scott Wong, Frank Thorp V and Brennan Leach report. But three years later, Congress still hasn’t passed any comprehensive legislation to rein in or create guardrails for the fast-moving technology. Even after countless committee hearings about AI and the formation of various commissions and task forces to study it, there’s not even any consensus in the House or the Senate about how to tackle the issue. Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon’s latest warnings about civilizational risk to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei set off fresh alarm bells and a flurry of activity on Capitol Hill, with Democrats and even some Republicans saying Congress faces a narrow time frame to act on AI. But despite the calls for action, it’s unlikely lawmakers will do anything before Election Day to address the dangers, even as experts say the technology’s capabilities are growing more powerful with each passing month. House GOP leaders have shown no urgency in prioritizing more sweeping AI regulations. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has mostly deferred to President Donald Trump, who has issued a series of executive orders on AI, most recently one that lays out a way for the federal government to conduct voluntary tests of powerful new AI systems before they are deployed. Johnson called AI an “important issue” Sunday on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” but “not one that we can rush into.” Meanwhile, Trump’s response to the calls to slow AI growth in the name of safety included downplaying the need for any congressional action. He posted Monday on Truth Social that the only control needed is “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump returned to the internet Monday afternoon to post again about the subject, NBC News’ Megan Brand reported, writing that “AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX” and that AI would be “the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History — Bigger than Oil, Gold, Diamonds, or even the Internet.” Johnson also said Monday that he expects Trump to “summon” AI executives to a meeting soon. Slowly but clearly, the 2028 election is already getting started Analysis by Natasha Korecki And so it begins. With 50 days to go until consequential midterm elections that will determine the balance of power in Congress, some on the left are zeroing in on 2028. Two progressive groups — Progressive Democrats of America and RootsAction — say that while they’re indeed focused on the midterms, it was imperative to reveal Monday that they’re ready to embrace Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Ro Khanna of California as potential Democratic presidential nominees. Of course, we see some version of this every four years. Progressive Democrats of America was behind a “Run Bernie Run” campaign before Bernie Sanders’ 2016 presidential run, and RootsAction put its own twist on the endeavor in 2022, attempting to “undraft” then-President Joe Biden from running for re-election with its “Don’t Run Joe” effort. Together, the activists behind the newly unveiled RunRoRunAOC.org make a far smaller push than, say, the Ready for Hillary super PAC endeavor in 2016. What’s significant here is that at least some of the Sanders faithful are signaling ground-level energy for both Khanna and Ocasio-Cortez, meaning they see either as suitable to run in the so-called Bernie lane. It’s an important distinction in a moment when the party is bucking more establishment Democrats. Ocasio-Cortez is still weighing the possibility of running for the Senate or for president in 2028. But in the meantime, she is drawing notice with trips to the South and stops speaking before Black voters. Khanna likewise has traveled extensively in ways that suggest his 2028 interest, including appearing at events with Rep. Jim Clyburn, the South Carolina Democratic kingmaker. The groups are pushing either or both to run, not suggesting that they run as a ticket. That’s with some hope that the two can help push the national conversation to the left, with the groups noting in their statement that “we believe their presence in the race is crucial to foster debate on healthcare, jobs, AI, militarism and the U.S. relationship with Israel.” Coming out this early to elevate Khanna and Ocasio-Cortez does something else. It works to pre-empt the party establishment from locking in more moderate Democratic front-runners. We’ve also seen this before: a mountain of early polling that creates an impression of an inevitable nominee. The joint statement from RootsAction and Progressive Democrats of America says that “most of the Democrats whose names now crowd the field have been war enablers, go-slow reformers or status quo protectors.” MORE: China dismisses AI slowdown calls and blasts ‘fearmongering’ from U.S. tech leaders That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Scott Bland. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: 'MAGA Act' could rip House seats from Dem states ahead of next presidential race
articles.summary: The House GOP proposal would count only citizens for apportionment, with a CIS report saying noncitizens gave Democrat states a net 14 seats.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A new House GOP proposal targeting the nation's congressional map could kneecap blue states and dramatically change their representation on Capitol Hill. Rep. Andrew Clyde, R-Ga., is introducing legislation that would only count citizens when deciding how many House representatives each state gets, called the Make Apportionment Great Again (MAGA) Act. It would be a fundamental change in congressional representation across the country, particularly hitting states where the most noncitizens live. The U.S. census has traditionally sought to count all people living within the country's borders, regardless of citizenship or even lawful status. WHERE TRUMP, GOP VS DEMOCRATS REDISTRICTING BATTLE HEADS NEXT IN WAKE OF KEY COURT RULINGS According to the U.S. census website, immigrants — both citizens and noncitizens — make up a fifth of the population in California, New Jersey, New York and Florida. Illegal immigrants living in sanctuary jurisdictions are also in theory counted by the census. A 2024 report by the Center for Immigration Studies (CIS) said immigrants, both legal and illegal, resulted in a "net increase" of 14 seats in Democrat-leaning states. Republican states had 10 fewer seats than they otherwise would have, the report said. MORE THAN A QUARTER-MILLION NONCITIZENS MAY BE REGISTERED TO VOTE IN 4 KEY STATES, DHS ALLEGES The legislation would not require a new census after 2020, instead forcing states to rely on existing records to reapportion by sometime in 2027. It would, however, add a new question to the 2030 census, asking people whether they are a U.S. citizen, U.S. national but not a citizen, an alien lawfully residing in the United States, or an alien unlawfully residing in the United States. RNC LEGAL VICTORY CLEARS NORTH CAROLINA VOTER ROLL PURGE OF NONCITIZENS THROUGH JURY RESPONSES But Clyde's bill could see a significant legal battle in the courts, even if passed. The 14th Amendment to the Constitution states that House seats will be apportioned after "counting the whole number of persons in each State," not specifying citizenship status. It could invite challenges from pro-immigrant groups and left-wing organizations that have long been critical of GOP election efforts. JACKSON ACCUSES THOMAS OF ECHOING INFAMOUSLY RACIST COURT DECISION IN BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CLASH Clyde's bill comes after a video clip resurfaced in July that appears to show Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., claiming she needs more immigrants in her district "just for redistricting purposes." The video, from a 2021 House Foreign Affairs Committee briefing, shows longtime Democrat Clarke suggesting that the local Haitian community in Brooklyn could "absorb a significant number of these migrants." "When I hear my colleagues talk about, you know, the doors of the inn being closed, no room in the inn, I’m saying, you know, I need more people in my district, just for redistricting purposes and those members could clearly fit here," said Clarke. articles.title: Seven-figure blitz as GOP embraces push to compete with China in booming new tech space
articles.summary: Alliance for a Better Future targets Bernie Sanders and AOC in new AI ads while praising three GOP lawmakers for balancing innovation and safeguards.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Three sitting Republican lawmakers, all facing midterm elections for U.S. Senate in less than two months, are paving the way for a pro-artificial intelligence push as Washington looks to balance regulation with American innovation despite the public's increasing skepticism over the emerging technology. The conservative Alliance for a Better Future (ABF) is pouring millions into backing the campaigns of Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, according to new ads shared exclusively with Fox News Digital ahead of their release. The lawmakers, ABF says, mirror President Donald Trump's balanced stance on applying both safeguards and common sense to AI developments. When speaking on the topic in June, Trump said, "[AI] can be used for tremendous good, mostly good and some bad. And the bad we have to stop." TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATES SCORE MAJOR BOOST FROM DEEP-POCKETED AI SUPER PAC IN UPCOMING PRIMARIES The advertisements come as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei over the weekend warned the industry that his company helps lead to give safety measures more time to catch up with rapidly advancing AI capabilities. Just days earlier an Anthropic researcher resigned while publicly raising concerns about the technology's risks. Anthropic is most known for its LLM AI Claude, one of the leading chatbots in the U.S. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, the father of ChatGPT, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis all expressed support for Amodei’s stance on slowing the pace of AI development. Trump on Monday rejected the calls for implementing safeguards and restrictions on AI, arguing the technology needs a "STRONG AND SMART" president rather than added restraints. The new advertisements, which will run throughout September, follow the ABF's previously unreported $1 million donation made to MAGA Inc. last week to promote candidates who share the group's values of pushing both innovation and security in emerging technologies like AI. But the ads aren't limited to praising Republicans — they also take shots at the perceived risks ABF believes could result from allowing socialist lawmakers like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., to lead policies dictating the direction of AI. SANDERS PUSHES 'DEATH PENALTY' FOR CRUCIAL US INDUSTRY THAT COULD GIVE ADVANTAGE TO FOREIGN ADVERSARIES "The same people who consistently fail you will write an AI rulebook for their benefit," the advertisement reads as images ofs of Sanders, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., appear on screen. Security concerns have been top of mind for many Americans and AI experts as the United States races to stay ahead of China in technology developments, with worry that the rapidly increasing growth of AI poses national and cybersecurity threats. "The only way we win the AI race against China is to build a technology that is trusted by the American people," ABF CEO Janet Kelly said in a statement to Fox News Digital on the new ad buys. "We cannot cede this responsibility to Socialists like Bernie Sanders who have a track record of destroying our economy and palling around with our enemies," she continued. "Conservatives like Susan Collins, Roger Marshall, and Ashley Hinson know the time is now to enact an agenda that ensures AI is built with American values." Sanders’ office did not reply to Fox News Digital’s request for comment on being singled out in the campaign ads. MIKE JOHNSON REJECTS AI MORATORIUM OVER CHINA THREAT AS CONSERVATIVE ACTIVIST DEMANDS GUARDRAILS Kelly, the former Secretary of Health in Virginia, warned that China will "cheat and steal and lie" to beat the U.S. in the AI race in a policy event hosted by Breitbart news last week. She emphasized the need for America to be both diligent and urgent in developing this technology at a pace that puts the U.S. above foreign adversaries. Collins, Marshall and Hinson have each backed policies that align with ABF’s goal to pursue AI development with protections that work to combat any emerging risks. Hinson has argued that the U.S. must maintain its technological edge over Beijing while being thorough in analyzing AI's risks. Marshall acknowledged AI as a tool to assist, not replace American workers — also backing measures addressing its workforce and energy impacts. Collins has supported federal investment in advanced computing while championing in Maine safeguards against deceptive AI-generated election content. TRUMP-ENDORSED HINSON SECURES IOWA SENATE NOMINATION AS DEMOCRATS EYE GOP SEAT ABF is a conservative AI policy organization that believes that as the technology continues to rapidly develop, American values should be prioritized — protecting children, the economy and national security. The three GOP lawmakers are all Republican nominees for Senate seats in the upcoming midterm elections for their respective states. articles.title: Alito, Thomas shred 'Hail Mary' challenge to federal ballot mail rules in dissent
articles.summary: Justice Samuel Alito called the Supreme Court's refusal to lift a universal injunction against Trump's mail-in ballot rules incorrect in a sharp dissent.
articles.body: Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas firmly dissented Monday as the Supreme Court denied a request by President Donald Trump's administration for relief from a universal injunction against its mail-in ballot rules. The dissent, which Alito authored and Thomas joined, argued that the plaintiffs in the case were relying on claims that the court had previously identified as weak and unlikely to succeed. "The Court incorrectly denies the Government’s application for a stay of a universal injunction that bars implementation of a final rule concerning election ballot mail," Alito wrote. "Some of the plaintiffs lack standing, while the remainder are pursuing a claim that this Court has recently called a ‘Hail Mary pass’ that ‘rarely succeeds.'" SUPREME COURT REJECTS TRUMP BID TO REVIVE STRICT MAIL-BALLOT RULES BEFORE MIDTERMS "The Government has made the showings necessary for a stay, so I respectfully dissent," he concluded. The Court's Monday order went unsigned, but Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote a concurrence that allowed room for a potential Trump victory down the line. He nevertheless argued that it is too close to Election Day to realistically implement the rules for the 2026 midterm elections. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT REJECTS TRUMP BID TO ENFORCE MAIL BALLOT ORDER AHEAD OF MIDTERM ELECTIONS "In my view, based on the briefing the Court has received at this interim stage, there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service’s statutory authority," Kavanaugh wrote. "But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections." Kavanaugh's concurrence echoes Alito's dissent in acknowledging the expansive authority the USPS holds to regulate the collection, handling, transportation and delivery of mail. USPS WOULDN'T DELIVER BALLOTS IN STATES THAT REFUSE TO FORK OVER MAIL-IN VOTER INFO UNDER PROPOSED RULE The Trump rules would require federal ballot mail to be sent in envelopes bearing an election-mail logo, capable of being scanned by high-speed equipment and carrying a barcode unique to each voter. State and local election officials would also be required to submit envelope designs to the Postal Service for review and upload basic voter information to an online USPS portal. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Under the USPS rule, mailings that failed to comply would not be accepted and would instead be returned to election officials to correct and resubmit. Fox News' Stepheny Price and Shannon Bream contributed to this report.

articles.title: Smithsonian’s dark take on America exposed: Washington dubbed ‘town destroyer,’ Revolutionary War ‘dangerous'
articles.summary: The Smithsonian Institution's American Indians museum labels George Washington a "town destroyer" while omitting key context about the attacks.
articles.body: NEW YORK — A Smithsonian museum in Manhattan presents a sharply critical account of George Washington, the Revolutionary War and America’s early years, while some historical context that complicates that narrative is omitted or given less prominent treatment, Fox News Digital found. The findings come as the Smithsonian faces heightened scrutiny from the Trump administration over how it presents American history. President Donald Trump has ordered a review of the institution’s exhibits and educational materials as part of an effort to change what his administration says is an overly negative portrayal of the country’s history. Fox News Digital visited the Manhattan branch of the National Museum of the American Indian earlier in September and found exhibits that emphasize the destruction suffered by Native communities while offering comparatively little context about the conflicts and events surrounding American military campaigns. One display near the center of the museum’s "Native New York" exhibit features an illustration of Washington’s profile — similar to the one that appears on quarters — over a label that reads "town destroyer." TRUMP GIVES SMITHSONIAN DAYS TO REPLACE 'STRANGE MODERNIST SCULPTURE' WITH FOUNDING FATHER The description underneath the image recounts how "American armies destroyed 40 Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) towns and burned their harvests while residents fled," noting that "the Haudenosaunee still call George Washington and all U.S. presidents Hanadahguyus. The name means ‘town destroyer.’" The panel does not mention the raids on American settlements that led to the campaign or explain why Washington ordered the attack. "The American destruction of the Six Nations' homelands came as a result of the destructive raids carried out by the Indians and American loyalists on the frontiers of New York and Pennsylvania in 1778," an excerpt from the National Park Service reads. "The raids crippled the American Continental Army by depriving it of food and manpower and spread terror by destroying frontier settlements and taking prisoners." The exhibit comes as the Trump administration continues its broader dispute with the Smithsonian over how the institution presents American history. Specifically, the president has taken issue with the institution allegedly seeking to divert the telling of American history "away from America’s Founding and the Founders and towards a narrative of a deeply flawed creation of the country." SMITHSONIAN SHOWDOWN INTENSIFIES AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ISSUES A STARK NEW WARNING The administration has threatened changes to Smithsonian funding and federal-agency support as it presses the institution to alter what it describes as divisive or historically inaccurate portrayals of the country. Many of the other exhibits in the museum take a similar line to the display on Washington, highlighting the alleged brutality of American settlers while downplaying the violence of natives. One placard, recounting the history of the Iroquois between 1779 and 1804 from the point of view of a native woman, states that "it was peaceful, she said, until the white men began their revolution." For roughly 100 years, between 1609 and 1701, the Iroquois were engaged in a series of conflicts with other native tribes over access to animal pelts. Even before the Trump administration’s current dispute with the Smithsonian, the National Museum of the American Indian in Washington, D.C., attracted criticism over how it presents American history. "​​In recent years, I have been chronicling the evolution of the ‘identity museum’ … designed to affirm a particular group’s claims, outline its accomplishments, boost its pride," a cultural critic wrote for the New York Times in 2010. "The National Museum of the American Indian in Washington — a pioneering example of the genre — jettisons Western scholarship and tells its own story, leading one tribe to solemnly describe its earliest historical milestone: ‘Birds teach people to call for rain.’" LEGAL EXPERT CALLS FOR SMITHSONIAN LEADERSHIP OVERHAUL OVER ‘SELF-LOATHING’ PORTRAYAL OF HISTORY: ‘IT’S BILE’ "Through a gauze of romance, that museum portrays an impossibly peace-loving, harmonious, homogeneous, pastoral world that preceded the invasion of white people — a vision with far less detail and insight than the old natural history museums once provided," the critic continued. The exhibits acknowledge some conflicts involving Native tribes but focus far more heavily on the violence inflicted on them than on the events that led to the fighting. The museum also maintains a catalog of online materials geared towards middle school students that generally take the same editorial line. Teachers, for instance, are instructed to show a video to students that opens by saying that "the American War for independence was such a disruptive and dangerous project." It goes on to frame the actions of American colonists negatively, referring to them as trespassers and squatters. WATCH: SMITHSONIAN DIRECTOR ADMITS SHE SEES HISTORY AS ‘TOOL’ OF ‘SOCIAL JUSTICE’ AFTER EXPLOSIVE HEARING In several displays dealing with the Revolutionary War, the exhibit portrays American actions toward Native allies in sharply negative terms. A video display near the beginning of the exhibit claims, unequivocally, that an American soldier shot and killed Chief White Eyes, a Lenape chief who had allied with the Americans. The cause of White Eyes’ death, however, is historically contested — something the museum outlines in relatively small text underneath the video display, which states that White Eyes was "probably" murdered by an American soldier. The museum is housed within the Alexander Hamilton U.S. Custom House, a building formerly used for collecting trade duties and named after the Founding Father to commemorate his role as the first secretary of the Treasury. HISTORIAN BLASTS SMITHSONIAN'S ACTIVISM SHIFT AFTER FIRST VISIT IN OVER A DECADE: 'COMPLETELY DIFFERENT PLACE' Just before exiting the building, visitors pass a museum store where several books present sharply critical accounts of American history. "An Indigenous Peoples’ History of the United States," for instance, is displayed prominently on the store shelves. Among other things, the book criticizes Americans for having a "cult-like" dedication to the Constitution, suggests that the United States was founded upon White supremacy and genocide and claims that the federal government is still carrying out ethnic cleansing against natives. A graphic novel adaptation of the text marketed toward younger readers was also available. Other titles on display included "Stealing America: The Hidden Story of Indigenous Slavery in US History," "An Afro-Indigenous History of the United States," a tome about the "two spirit" gender identity and a children’s picture book about Deb Haaland, President Joe Biden’s interior secretary. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Smithsonian did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday.

articles.title: Live updates: Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon to join diverse speakers at ‘Pro-Human’ AI conference
articles.summary: Live updates and the latest news as lawmakers, actors and religious leaders join ‘Pro-Human’ summit to discuss curbs on artificial intelligence, while Trump has characterized concerns about AI development a “hoax.”
articles.body:
What to know today 'PRO-HUMAN' AI CONFERENCE: Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and former Trump White House aide Steve Bannon will be among the attendees at a conference in Washington, D.C., today, dubbed the Pro-Human Assembly, aimed at pressing for new policies to place some curbs on the rapidly accelerating development of artificial intelligence. TRUMP DOWNPLAYS CONCERNS: President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has characterized concerns about AI safety as a "hoax," saying in a phone call to Nvidia's Jensen Huang, which the CEO put on speakerphone at an industry summit, that the U.S. had to beat China in AI innovation and development. ECONOMIC IMPACT: The calls from tech executives and world leaders to put some brakes on AI development are raising questions about whether a tech slowdown could rein in U.S. economic growth.
